title: Account Lifecycle: Joiner, Mover, Leaver
subtitle: How an identity at the organization is created, changed and removed so that access always matches a person’s current relationship with the organization.
tierText: Tier 2 — Advanced Technical Services. Onboarding prep already sits with Tier 2 under the published tier model. Tier 4 owns this document.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend Head of IT, with HR concurrence on §5 intake and §7.3 retention ]
audience: IT Account Services and IT administrators. HR and hiring managers act as requesters.
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and on any change to the HR and user system of record, Entra ID, or the HR onboarding process.

steps.text: Validate the request against the HR and user system of record. If the record does not exist, return it to HR — who own the process and can resolve it at source. Do not create a manual identity to bridge the gap.
steps.label: Validate the request against the HR and user…

steps.text: Create the identity per ACC-02. Do not deviate from the naming standard to accommodate a personal preference or a departmental habit; raise a change against ACC-02 instead. Local deviations are how a convention becomes contested.
steps.label: Create the identity per ACC-02

steps.text: Assign the licence for the account class per §3 and record it (M365-20).
steps.label: Assign the licence for the account…

steps.text: Confirm that dynamic group membership resolves. Dynamic groups derive from the HR and user system of record attributes, so an identity created before its record in the HR and user system of record is complete will land outside its groups and the person will appear to have no access on day one. Verify, do not assume (M365-04).
steps.label: Confirm that dynamic group membership resolves…

steps.text: Grant the role default entitlements only. Anything beyond the default requires the manager’s written approval recorded on the ticket — not a verbal agreement, and not an inference from what the previous post-holder had.
steps.label: Grant the role default entitlements only

steps.text: Where the role needs a departmental shared mailbox, raise it through M365-03 so the mailbox acquires a named owner. Do not add the person directly.
steps.label: The role needs a departmental shared mailbox?

gate.cond: the role needs a departmental shared mailbox
gate.then: raise it through M365-03 so the mailbox acquires a named owner

steps.text: Provision the device per DEV-01 and record the assignment against the person, including asset tag.
steps.label: Provision the device per DEV-01…

steps.text: Issue a Temporary Access Pass rather than a plain password where the platform supports it, so that first sign-in forces MFA registration and no shared secret ever exists in an email (ACC-03).
steps.label: Issue a Temporary Access Pass rather…

steps.text: Deliver credentials in person or to the manager. Never to a personal email address. A reset request from a personal email account, on behalf of a differently-named person, is a classic social-engineering move; the control that stops that class of request is ACC-06, and it starts here.
steps.label: Deliver credentials in person…

steps.text: Record on the ticket: account name, licence assigned, groups resolved, device asset tag, MFA enrollment deadline, and who received the credentials.
steps.label: Record on the ticket

steps.sub: 5.3 Day one — actions by the person
steps.text: Sign in, set a password meeting ACC-04, and register at least two MFA methods within 24 hours (ACC-03).
steps.label: Sign in, set a password meeting…

steps.sub: 5.3 Day one — actions by the person
steps.text: Read and acknowledge the organization’s acceptable use policy, including the prohibition on credential sharing. Where that policy already exists, ACC-15 governs how it is presented and evidenced at this step rather than replacing it.
steps.label: Read and acknowledge the acceptable use policy…

steps.sub: 5.3 Day one — actions by the person
steps.text: Confirm mailbox, Teams and file access. Report any gap on the original provisioning ticket rather than opening a new one, so that the joiner record stays in one place.
steps.label: Confirm mailbox, Teams and file access

callouts.title: The governing principle
lines: A role change is a removal followed by an addition. The addition always happens, because the person needs it and will ask. The removal is the step that gets skipped — and it is the step that matters. Every stale entitlement in the tenant was once a legitimate grant to someone whose role subsequently changed.

steps.text: Retrieve the person’s current entitlements in full: group memberships (assigned and dynamic), shared mailbox membership, SharePoint and OneDrive permissions, mailbox and calendar delegations, application roles, privileged roles, and device assignments.
steps.label: Retrieve the person’s current entitlements…

steps.text: Produce the delta against the incoming role’s default entitlement set. Attach it to the ticket. This list is the deliverable of the step, not a by-product.
steps.label: Produce the delta against the incoming…

steps.text: Remove every entitlement not in the incoming role default. Retention of a legacy entitlement requires the new manager’s written justification on the ticket and expires automatically after 90 days unless renewed.
steps.label: Remove every entitlement not…

steps.text: Add the incoming role’s defaults.
steps.label: Add the incoming role’s defaults

steps.text: Where the person owned a shared mailbox, Team or SharePoint site for the outgoing department, reassign ownership before removing their access. An unowned site is where link rot starts; broken-link tickets sit past SLA for exactly this reason.
steps.label: The person owned a shared mailbox?

gate.cond: the person owned a shared mailbox
gate.then: Team or SharePoint site for the outgoing department, reassign ownership before removing their access

steps.text: Where the person sponsored guest accounts, reassign sponsorship or expire the guests (ACC-10).
steps.label: The person sponsored guest accounts?

gate.cond: the person sponsored guest accounts
gate.then: reassign sponsorship or expire the guests (ACC-10)

steps.text: Update the device assignment if the device moves with the department, and re-scope any device-based configuration.
steps.label: The device moves with the department?

gate.cond: the device moves with the department
gate.then: and re-scope any device-based configuration

steps.text: Record the before and after entitlement lists on the ticket. This is the evidence the quarterly access review in ACC-17 depends on.
steps.label: Record the before and after entitlement…

callouts.title: Two years is a floor, not a window
lines: Mailbox and OneDrive content — both files and email — is retained for a MINIMUM of two years after separation. There is no maximum. Nothing is deleted at the two-year mark; two years is the point before which deletion is not permitted at all.
Deletion after that floor is a deliberate, approved act with a recorded reason, not an automatic expiry. The default in the absence of a decision is to keep.

callouts.title: Mail and files do not behave the same way, and the difference decides the procedure
lines: A two-year floor with no maximum is the right call for an organization that keeps records. Implemented naively — by leaving the account licensed — it means paying for a licence for every person who ever left, forever. So the floor has to be delivered without a licence. For mail that is straightforward. For files it needs a deliberate choice between four routes, only one of which is free.

MAIL. A shared mailbox needs no licence up to 50 GB, and an inactive mailbox under a Microsoft 365 retention hold survives licence removal indefinitely. Both are documented, supported mechanisms. The floor is met at no cost.

FILES. An unlicensed OneDrive is not simply dormant. Microsoft places unlicensed OneDrive accounts into read-only mode after 60 unlicensed days and archives them after 93, and a cumulative 365-day nonpayment clock carries a deletion risk beyond that. Retention policies and legal holds ARE honoured through the archived state — but only while archive billing is enabled; unpaid, the content is at risk at 365 days despite any hold. Reassigning the OneDrive’s owner does not change this: Microsoft states that enforcement does not use the owner property to validate licensing, and that changing it is an unsupported state.

IF YOUR TENANT IS AN EDUCATION OR NONPROFIT TENANT, check Microsoft’s current guidance: some enforcement changes have been stated not to apply to EDU customers. The scope of that exclusion is not stated cleanly enough to build a two-year retention commitment on. Obtaining it in writing from Microsoft is an open prerequisite (§9.2) and would materially simplify this procedure.

THEREFORE, unless an exclusion has been confirmed in writing for your tenant, the default is to MOVE the records: institutional content goes into the departmental SharePoint site during the 30-day manager window, where a retention policy holds it and colleagues can actually use it. It costs nothing, depends on no billing toggle, and is what Microsoft itself recommends for a OneDrive with no active owner. The three alternatives — a longer tenant active-storage period, paid archive, or a retained licence — are set out in M365-16 §5 with their costs.

steps.text: Disable sign-in. Do not delete the account. Deletion destroys the mailbox and the OneDrive with it, and both are frequently needed after the person has gone.
steps.label: Disable sign-in

steps.text: Revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and remove registered MFA methods. A disabled account with a live token is not disabled.
steps.label: Revoke active sessions and refresh tokens…

steps.text: Remove all group memberships, shared mailbox membership, delegations, SharePoint and OneDrive permissions, application roles and privileged roles.
steps.label: Remove all group memberships, shared mailbox…

steps.text: Reassign ownership of every SharePoint site, Team and shared mailbox the person owned, before their access is removed. Record the new owner.
steps.label: Reassign ownership of every SharePoint site…

steps.text: Handle the mailbox. Where the department needs continued access, convert it to a shared mailbox — this preserves all mail and calendar and needs no licence below 50 GB. Where it does not, place the mailbox under a retention hold and make it inactive. Either way the sign-in stays blocked and the password is reset, because a converted shared mailbox still answers to the departed person’s original credentials until it does not. Do not configure forwarding to a personal address under any circumstances. The order in §7.3 is not optional.
steps.label: Handle the mailbox

steps.text: Handle the OneDrive: grant the manager delegated access for 30 days and MOVE institutional records into the department’s SharePoint site inside that window. For files, unlike mail, the move is the retention — an unlicensed OneDrive is not a preserved OneDrive (§7.3). The alternative is a bespoke recovery project for one departure (M365-12).
steps.label: Handle the OneDrive

steps.text: Reclaim the licence only once the mailbox is shared or inactive under hold AND the OneDrive move is confirmed complete — in that order, verified, not assumed (M365-20 Appendix A).
steps.label: Reclaim the licence only once…

steps.text: Confirm device return per DEV-15. Before wiping, verify the BitLocker recovery key is escrowed in Entra ID. Some devices may have no escrowed key at all, so this check must be performed and recorded rather than presumed (DEV-03).
steps.label: Confirm device return per DEV-15…

steps.text: Expire or reassign every guest account the person sponsored.
steps.label: Expire or reassign every guest account…

steps.text: Record completion of each step on the ticket. A leaver ticket with unrecorded steps is not closed, whatever its status field says.
steps.label: Record completion of each step…

appendices.head: Appendix A — Help desk verification script
rows: “Before I can make any change to the account, I need to verify who I’m speaking to. I can do that in person at the service desk, or on a short video call — whichever is easier for you.”

If the request arrived from a non-the organization address: “I can’t action a request from an outside address, but I can help you directly. Are you able to join a quick video call?” Do not proceed on the email thread.
On video: “Please turn your camera on and hold your photo ID up to the camera.” Check the name and photo against the directory record.

“Without me prompting you, can you tell me two of the following: your HR/client record ID, your department, your manager’s name, or the asset tag on your organization laptop.” Do not list which one you are expecting. Note which facts they gave.
If they cannot: “I can accept confirmation from your manager instead. May I copy them on this ticket?” That is Tier 3, and the manager must reply from their own organization account.
Before acting, check: is the account actually disabled, unlicensed, or blocked by policy rather than by password? Run Appendix B first.
Act. Prefer a Temporary Access Pass over a temporary password.
Record on the ticket: verification tier, facts relied on, action taken, confirmed §8 cause.
Confirm the person has signed in successfully. Then close.

appendices.head: Appendix B — Lockout triage card
rows: Does the sign-in fail everywhere, immediately, including on site?
Yes → AD lockout. Unlock, then hunt the stale credential.
Does it work from one place or client but not another?
Yes → Entra smart lockout. Check the source IP; unfamiliar burst → §10.
Is the password accepted but the second factor never arrives?
Yes → MFA method problem. Verify per §6, re-register per §5.4. Do NOT reset the password.
Did they get a specific policy or compliance message?
Yes → Conditional Access or risk block. Read the sign-in log; fix the condition, not the password.
Does sign-in succeed but one app or portal deny access?
Yes → not a lockout. Licence, group, or application. Reclassify the ticket.
Has this account been here before in the last 90 days?
Yes → go to the §9 ladder before restoring.

appendices.head: Appendix C — End-user quick reference
rows: You forgot your password
Use the self-service reset link in any IT email signature or on the IT pages. It works without contacting anyone, provided you registered two methods.
You are getting a new phone
Register a method on the new phone BEFORE you wipe or trade in the old one. This takes two minutes and avoids everything below.
You already lost the phone with your only method
Contact the service desk. You will be asked to verify your identity in person or on a short video call with photo ID. This is not a formality and cannot be waived.
You think your account has been accessed by someone else
Contact the service desk immediately and say so explicitly. Do not change the password first — IT needs to see the sign-in trail before it changes.
Someone asks for your password or an MFA code
Never provide it. IT will never ask for either. Report the request to the service desk.
You are locked out and it is urgent
Say so, and still expect to verify. Urgency is the most common pretext used against help desks, so the verification step applies especially when time is short.

steps.label: For a population

steps.label: Record the key ID, not…

steps.label: Trigger a key rotation from Intune…

gate.cond: a device cannot be brought into escrow and must be recovered

callouts.title: The hourly re-notification is switched off, and that is the first change to make
lines: It is producing noise and nothing else. A handful of tickets re-announcing themselves every hour trains everyone who receives it to filter the whole category, which means the one notice that mattered is also filtered.
This is the cheapest item in the whole catalogue to implement and it should not wait for the rest of this document to be approved.

The oldest breached ticket is the test case: it is either accepted with a real date, redirected, or closed as will-not-do and the requester told. It is not left as it is.

steps.label: Configure the tier and priority fields…

title: Password Standard & Self-Service Password Reset
subtitle: What a password must be, why one gets rejected, and how a person resets their own without contacting anybody.
tierText: Tier 1 — the Service Desk (“the front door”, the service desk address). Configuration is Tier 3; the conversation is Tier 1’s.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Every six months while a move to Entra is under way, then annually.

steps.text: Confirm the tenant configuration: two methods required, security questions NOT enabled as a method, and the reset actually completing end to end on a real test account.
steps.label: Confirm the tenant configuration

steps.text: Enable for a pilot group of IT staff first. Reset a real password. Do not proceed on the strength of the configuration screen looking correct.
steps.label: Enable for a pilot group…

steps.text: Enable the Windows sign-in screen option for Entra-joined devices, and test it on a device that is genuinely locked out rather than one that is merely signed out.
steps.label: Enable the Windows sign-in screen option…

steps.text: Extend to staff. Measure assisted-reset volume weekly against the April–August baseline.
steps.label: Extend to staff

steps.text: Extend to everyone else, the largest population and the largest prize. Expect a temporary rise in tickets as people discover the feature; this is not failure.
steps.label: Extend to everyone else, the largest population…

steps.text: Put the reset link in the mail signature of every service desk reply about access, on the knowledge base portal, and on the Tier 1 desk card. A capability nobody knows about does not reduce anything.
steps.label: Put the reset link…

steps.text: Verify identity per ACC-06 and record the tier used.
steps.label: Verify identity per ACC-06 and record…

steps.text: Confirm the password is actually the problem (ACC-05 §2).
steps.label: Confirm the password is actually…

steps.text: Prefer a Temporary Access Pass over a temporary password. A temporary password does not expire on use and will still work weeks later.
steps.label: Prefer a Temporary Access Pass…

steps.text: Where a temporary password is unavoidable, require change at next sign-in and deliver it in person, on a verified video call, or to the manager. Never to a personal address and never in the ticket body.
steps.label: A temporary password is unavoidable?

gate.cond: a temporary password is unavoidable
gate.then: require change at next sign-in and deliver it in person, on a verified video call, or to the manager

steps.text: Confirm the person has signed in successfully before closing. The outcome is access, not a reset.
steps.label: Confirm the person has signed…

steps.text: While you have them: if they have fewer than two methods registered, get the second one registered now. That is what stops the next call.
steps.label: While you have them

appendices.head: Appendix A — Desk card: “why was my password rejected?”
rows: Doesn’t meet requirements
“Try a longer passphrase — three or four unrelated words works best.”
Can’t reuse it
“Recent passwords are blocked. Try something genuinely different rather than adding a number.”
Worked before, won’t work now
Take the detail. If it happens twice, escalate — that may be a real policy mismatch.
Changed it, laptop wants the old one
“Connect to the network or VPN, then lock and unlock.” Not a password problem.
Keeps asking me to change it
Check for a temporary password; help them set a permanent one.
Just forgot it
aka.ms/sspr — stay on the call while they do it.
Forgot it, and has no MFA registered
Self-service cannot verify them. Verify per ACC-06, escalate to Tier 2 for a Temporary Access Pass.
Locked out rather than forgotten
Go to ACC-05. Do not reset — it will not clear a lockout.

appendices.head: Appendix B — End-user text for publication
rows: Resetting your password
Go to aka.ms/sspr. You will be verified through one of the security methods you registered, then asked for a new password. No need to contact anyone.
Choosing a password

Length matters more than symbols. Three or four unrelated words make a strong password that you can actually remember. Avoid anything containing the organization’s name, its mascot, a season or a year.
If reset does not work

You probably have fewer than two security methods registered, which means we cannot verify you automatically. Contact the service desk — you will be asked to confirm your identity in person or on a short video call with photo ID.
Register a second method now
The five minutes it takes today is what lets you fix your own account at 11pm the night before a deadline. Go to aka.ms/mysecurityinfo.
We will never ask for your password
Not by email, not on the phone, not in a ticket. Anyone who does is not IT — report it.

title: Account Lockout Triage & Repeat-Incident Escalation
subtitle: How to tell apart the five different things people report as “locked out”, and what happens when the same account comes back.
tierText: Tier 1 — the Service Desk. Escalates to Tier 2 Account Services, which holds the directory permissions.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Every six months while you are changing identity platforms, then annually.

flows.head: 3. Cause by cause — what to do

steps.text: Confirm the lockout flag. Do not reset the password — the password is probably fine.
steps.label: Confirm the lockout flag

steps.text: Escalate to Tier 2 to unlock. Tier 1 cannot unlock in Entra or AD.
steps.label: Escalate to Tier 2 to unlock

steps.text: Then find the source, which is the part that stops it recurring. A stale credential on a phone mail client, a mapped drive with a saved old password, or a scheduled task is the usual culprit. An account that locks out again within hours has a machine doing it, not a person.
steps.label: Then find the source, which…

steps.text: Record the source when found. A pattern across several accounts is a Tier 3 matter.
steps.label: Record the source when found

steps.text: Read the sign-in log: how many failures, from where, against what.
steps.label: Read the sign-in log

steps.text: Where the source is the person’s own location, wait out the lockout or have Tier 2 clear it, then address whatever is retrying.
steps.label: The source is the person’s own location?

gate.cond: the source is the person’s own location
gate.then: wait out the lockout or have Tier 2 clear it, then address whatever is retrying

steps.text: Where the source is an unfamiliar IP or country, stop treating this as a lockout. It is a possible compromise — go to ACC-03 §10 and notify Tier 3.
steps.label: The source is an unfamiliar IP?

gate.cond: the source is an unfamiliar IP or country
gate.then: stop treating this as a lockout

steps.text: Do not reset the password. It is not broken and resetting it adds a second problem.
steps.label: Do not reset the password

steps.text: Verify identity per ACC-06. This is the case most often exploited, because “I have a new phone” is entirely plausible and requires no story.
steps.label: Verify identity per ACC-06

steps.text: Escalate to Tier 2 for method re-registration, or a Temporary Access Pass where every method is gone (ACC-03 §5.4).
steps.label: Escalate to Tier 2 for method…

steps.text: Before closing, get a second method registered. This case is almost always a person who had only one.
steps.label: Get a second method registered

steps.sub: D — Conditional Access or risk block
steps.text: Read the policy name or risk detection in the sign-in log. The log says why; guessing wastes the contact.
steps.label: Read the policy name or risk…

steps.sub: D — Conditional Access or risk block
steps.text: Resolve the condition — device compliance, location, app, or risk state. A reset will not clear it and will mask the cause.
steps.label: Resolve the condition — device compliance…

steps.sub: D — Conditional Access or risk block
steps.text: Where the block is a device compliance failure, this is a device matter (DEV-02), not an account one.
steps.label: The block is a device compliance failure?

gate.cond: the block is a device compliance failure
gate.then: this is a device matter (DEV-02), not an account one

steps.sub: D — Conditional Access or risk block
steps.text: Where the same policy blocks several people in a day, escalate to Tier 3 immediately. That is a misconfiguration, not five user problems (ACC-03 §11).
steps.label: The same policy blocks several people?

gate.cond: the same policy blocks several people in a day
gate.then: escalate to Tier 3 immediately

steps.text: Reclassify the ticket. The category matters for measurement and travels with the ticket on escalation.
steps.label: Reclassify the ticket

steps.text: Check licence (M365-20), then group membership (M365-04), then the application itself (ACC-16).
steps.label: Check licence (M365-20), then group membership…

flows.name: Cause by cause — what to do

appendices.head: Appendix A — Triage card
rows: Does it fail everywhere, immediately, including on site?
Cause A — AD lockout. Escalate to unlock, then hunt the stale credential.
Does it work from somewhere else, or on another device?
Cause B — smart lockout. Read the source IP. Unfamiliar → ACC-03 §10.
Is the password accepted, and then the second factor never arrives?
Cause C — MFA method. Do NOT reset. Verify per ACC-06, escalate for re-registration.
Did they get a specific policy or compliance message?
Cause D — Conditional Access. Read the log; fix the condition, not the password.
Does sign-in succeed, but one app denies them?
Cause E — not a lockout. Reclassify: licence, group, or application.
Are they saying somebody else has been signing in?
Go to §4. Do not reset. Tier 2 first.
Has this account been here before in the last 90 days?
Go to Appendix B before restoring.

rows: 1st
Restore. Record cause. Brief on credential sharing. Register a second MFA method.
Nobody beyond the ticket.
2nd in 90 days
Restore. Review sign-in history. Re-register all methods. Flag for watch.
Tier 2.
3rd in 90 days
Treat as suspected compromise. Force reset, revoke sessions, re-register everything.
Their manager, in writing. Tier 3 decides; Tier 4 informed.
Sharing confirmed
Suspend per ACC-13. Do not restore pending referral.
HR, or whoever handles conduct. Tier 4 approves.
Compromise confirmed
Preserve audit data BEFORE remediating. Declare under GOV-03.
Tier 4 declares the incident.

title: Identity Verification Before Any Account Action
subtitle: How IT establishes that a person asking for access is who they say they are, before anyone touches the account.
tierText: Tier 1 — the Service Desk, and every tier that touches an account. No tier is exempt.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and after any attempted social-engineering incident.

steps.text: Every person at every tier who can take an account action reads this document and Appendix A before their first shift.
steps.label: Every person at every tier who…

steps.text: Tier 1 technicians re-read it every quarter, because people change and this is the tier attackers call.
steps.label: Tier 1 technicians re-read…

steps.text: The department runs one deliberate practice attempt per quarter — a colleague calls the desk with a plausible unverified request. The purpose is to find out whether the procedure holds, not to catch anybody out, and the result is discussed openly with no individual named.
steps.label: The department runs one deliberate practice…

steps.text: Every real attempt is written up and circulated, with the story of what the caller said. Specifics teach; policy statements do not.
steps.label: Every real attempt is written up…

appendices.head: Appendix A — The verification script
rows: “Before I make any change to the account, I need to check who I’m speaking to. I can do that here at the desk, or on a quick video call — whichever is easier for you.”
Request from a outside address? “I can’t action a request from an outside address, but I can help you directly. Can you join a short video call?” Do not continue on the email thread.
On video: “Please turn your camera on and hold your photo ID up.” Check name, photo, person. That is the whole check.
“Without me prompting you, tell me two things about your record here — anything you like.” Do NOT list what you are expecting. Note which two they gave.
Cannot do either? “I can accept confirmation from your manager instead — may I copy them on the ticket?” That is V3, and the manager must reply from their own work account.
Before acting: is the password even the problem? Run the ACC-05 triage card first.
Act. Prefer a Temporary Access Pass over a temporary password.
Record: verification tier, which facts they volunteered, action taken, and the confirmed ACC-05 cause.
Confirm they have signed in successfully. Then close.

appendices.head: Appendix B — What to say when declining
rows: Request from a personal address

“I’m not able to action account changes from an outside address — that’s the same rule that stops someone else doing it to your account. I can sort this out with you on a two-minute video call though. What works?”
They are in a hurry
“I understand, and I’d rather not slow you down — the check takes about ninety seconds and then I can get straight into it.”
A colleague asking on someone’s behalf

“I can’t make the change on someone else’s account, but if you can put me in touch with them directly I’ll get it done now. Or if you’re their manager, you can confirm their identity on the ticket and that works too.”
They push back on principle
“It’s our procedure rather than my call, and it applies to everybody — including our own staff. Let me get it done quickly and then we can fix the actual problem.”
They stay angry
“I hear you, and I’m not going to be able to waive it. Let me bring my supervisor in so you’re not stuck with me on this.” Then escalate. Do not negotiate.

steps.label: Configure send-as for the members who…

steps.label: At the review date, Tier 2…

steps.label: Temporary-worker membership is removed at the end…

appendices.head: Appendix A — Request form fields
rows: Requested address
Function-based, not person-based.
Purpose, in one sentence
Distinguishes a mailbox from a distribution list at the point of request.
Named owner (staff member)
The whole point. A department name is not an owner.
Named deputy owner
So the mailbox does not become an IT judgement call during annual leave.
Initial members
Each named individually.
Any temporary workers among them?
Triggers the end-date expiry in §7.1.
Does it receive sensitive data?
Customer records, payroll, health, conduct — triggers the §5 step 4 referral.
Send-as or send-on-behalf?
Default is send-as; §8 explains the difference.

appendices.head: Appendix B — Owner’s one-pager
rows: You now own a mailbox
You are the person who decides who can read and answer mail sent to this address. IT will administer it, but will not add anybody without your say-so.
To add somebody
Ask the service desk, naming the person. Please do it that way rather than by email thread — it means there is a record of who authorised it, which protects you as much as anyone.
Temporary workers
Their access ends automatically at the end of the engagement. If you want it to continue, you will be asked to approve it again — that is deliberate.
Once a year
We will send you the list of people who have access and ask you to confirm it is still right. It takes a minute and it is the main thing that stops access accumulating.
Before you leave or change role
Please tell us who should take over. A mailbox with no owner stops being answered, and nobody notices until an enquirer complains.
What recipients see
By default, replies appear to come from the department rather than from you personally. We can change that if you would rather.

title: Distribution List & Dynamic Group Standard
subtitle: How mail reaches a group of people at the organization, how dynamic membership is derived from the HR and user system of record, and what IT will not build.

flows.head: 6. Dynamic groups — how membership is actually derived

callouts.title: The two misunderstandings worth pre-empting
lines: First: “add this person to employees@”. Not possible, and not a limitation — it is what makes the group trustworthy. If they belong in it, their record says so.

Second: an alias on a group is not a second group. Adding sales-team@ as an alias of dept-sales@ does not create a different membership; it is the same list reachable by two addresses. This is the commonest alias confusion, and §9 addresses it directly.

steps.text: The HR and user system of record holds the authoritative record for every person. Directory attributes are populated from it.
steps.label: The HR and user system of record holds…

steps.text: A dynamic group holds a rule against those attributes, not a list of people. Nobody is “added to” a dynamic group, and asking IT to add somebody to one is asking for something that does not exist as an operation.
steps.label: A dynamic group holds a rule…

steps.text: Membership is evaluated when mail is sent. So a correction to somebody’s record in the HR and user system of record fixes their group membership — and, equally, a wrong record silently excludes them with no error anywhere.
steps.label: Membership is evaluated when mail…

steps.text: Which means: when a person is missing from a population group, the fault is almost never the group. It is the record. Fix the record (ACC-01 Rule 1).
steps.label: Which means

flows.name: Dynamic groups — how membership is actually derived

steps.text: IT maintains a register of every directory attribute, what it holds, what populates it, and what depends on it. Appendix B is the template.
steps.label: IT maintains a register of every…

steps.text: No attribute is committed to a new purpose without a Tier 4 decision recorded against M365-21.
steps.label: No attribute is committed…

steps.text: Before promising any dynamic group, Tier 3 checks the register. A promise made and then withdrawn costs more than a slow answer.
steps.label: Tier 3 checks the register

steps.text: Where the register shows no attribute available, the answer is §8 — and now it comes with a reason the requester can see.
steps.label: The register shows no attribute available?

gate.cond: the register shows no attribute available
gate.then: the answer is §8 — and now it comes with a reason the requester can see

steps.label: Manual distribution lists are reviewed annually…

steps.text: Dynamic groups do not need membership review, but their rules do — annually, and whenever the underlying attribute changes meaning.
steps.label: Dynamic groups do not need membership…

steps.text: The attribute register is reviewed annually and whenever a system is retired. A tool retiring in favour of Intune, for instance, may free the attribute that blocked a department’s request — which is worth knowing.
steps.label: The attribute register is reviewed annually…

An alias (M365-05). Minutes, not a project.
Have several people answer mail sent to one published address
A shared mailbox (M365-03).

Two objects, not one. Ask Tier 3.

rows: “A new email address”
Ask: should mail to your current address keep working, and should your outbound mail keep coming from it? Yes to both → alias.
An alias
Check it is not in use anywhere. Add it. Then tell them outbound mail still comes from the primary address.
To change their address because they prefer a different form
Offer an alias. It gives them the address they want without the consequences of a change.
To change their address after a legal name change
HR confirmation, then §4.2. Keep the old address as an alias permanently.
An alias that reaches different people from the current address
That is not an alias. It is a group or a mailbox — M365-04 or M365-03.
An address that used to belong to somebody else

ceo@ or similar for personal use

version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman

steps.text: Prefer moving the file to the departmental site over sharing it from your OneDrive. Sharing solves today; moving solves permanently.
steps.label: Prefer moving the file…

steps.label: Sharing is right?

gate.then: share with named people rather than with “anyone with the link”

steps.label: Set an expiry on any external…

steps.label: Never share anything of a sensitive…

steps.label: Talk to the person first

steps.text: Identify or create the destination: an existing departmental site, or a new one under M365-10 with a named owner.
steps.label: Identify or create the destination

steps.label: Move rather than copy

steps.label: Confirm permissions on the destination before…

appendices.head: Appendix A — End-user text
rows: Your OneDrive
Yours for drafts, working notes and personal copies. It is backed up and it is private to you unless you share something.
The one rule
If the organization would need a file after you left, it should not live only in your OneDrive. Put it in your department’s SharePoint site instead.
When to move it
When somebody else first needs it — not when it is finished. Waiting for “finished” is how documents stay put for years.
Not sure where it goes?
Ask the service desk. It is a thirty-second answer and nobody minds being asked.
Sharing
Share with named people rather than “anyone with the link”, and put an expiry on anything going outside the organization.
If you are leaving
Your manager gets access to your OneDrive for 30 days so anything the department needs can be moved. If you have followed the rule above, there will be nothing to do.

title: Phishing Reporting & Email Threat Response
subtitle: What a person does when a message looks wrong, and what IT does after they report it.
tierText: Tier 2 — Advanced Technical Services, which already owns malware containment. Escalates to Tier 3 and Tier 4.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Every six months. Attacker technique changes faster than most standards.

steps.text: Establish what the message is trying to obtain: credentials, a payment, a file, or a reply that starts a conversation. This determines everything that follows.
steps.label: Establish what the message is trying…

steps.text: Establish the blast radius. How many mailboxes received it? Search the tenant by sender, subject and URL — not by one of the three.
steps.label: Establish the blast radius

steps.text: Establish whether anybody interacted. Clicks and credential submissions are what turn a nuisance into an incident.
steps.label: Establish whether anybody interacted

steps.text: Classify: nuisance (spam, no credential objective), credential harvest, business email compromise, or malware delivery.
steps.label: Classify

steps.text: For anything other than nuisance, tell Tier 3 immediately and do not wait until containment is finished. Two people working in parallel is the point of a tier model.
steps.label: For anything other than nuisance, tell…

steps.text: Where credentials may have been submitted, this is a GOV-03 incident and Tier 4 is informed. Do not decide alone whether it is “serious enough”.
steps.label: Credentials may have been submitted?

gate.cond: credentials may have been submitted
gate.then: this is a GOV-03 incident and Tier 4 is informed

steps.text: Purge the message from every mailbox that received it, tenant-wide. Not only the reporter’s.
steps.label: Purge the message from every mailbox…

steps.text: Block the sender, the sending infrastructure and the URLs.
steps.label: Block the sender, the sending infrastructure…

steps.text: Check whether the same campaign arrived under other subjects or senders. Campaigns rarely send one variant.
steps.label: Check whether the same campaign arrived…

steps.text: Where one of your own accounts is sending it, that account is compromised. Disable sign-in, revoke sessions and tokens, and go to §5 — an internal sender is a much more serious situation than an external one because it defeats the banner and the recipient’s instincts.
steps.label: One of your own accounts is sending it?

gate.cond: one of your own accounts is sending it
gate.then: that account is compromised

steps.text: Record what was purged and when. This is the evidence for §6 and for any later question about who could have seen it.
steps.label: Record what was purged…

steps.text: Ask what they entered and where. A username alone is a different situation from a password, and a password plus an approved MFA prompt is different again.
steps.label: Ask what they entered and where

steps.text: Reset the password and revoke every session and refresh token. A password reset alone does not end a session that is already established.
steps.label: Reset the password and revoke every…

steps.text: Remove and re-register MFA methods. An attacker who got in may have added their own method, which survives a password reset — this is the step most often missed.
steps.label: Remove and re-register MFA methods

steps.text: Check for mailbox rules created by the attacker: auto-forwarding, auto-delete, or rules hiding replies. This is the standard persistence move and it is invisible to the user.
steps.label: Check for mailbox rules created…

steps.text: Check for new delegations, send-as grants, and OAuth application consents.
steps.label: Check for new delegations, send-as grants…

steps.text: Check what the mailbox sent while compromised, and whether it phished anybody else internally.
steps.label: Check what the mailbox sent while…

steps.text: Preserve the audit data before remediating where the sequence allows — Tier 3 decides the order when both matter (ACC-03 §10).
steps.label: Preserve the audit data before remediating…

steps.text: Tell the person plainly what was done and what to watch for. They will be anxious; a clear account helps, and it makes them likely to report faster next time.
steps.label: Tell the person plainly what was…

appendices.head: Appendix A — Triage card
rows: What is it after — credentials, money, a file, or a reply?
Credentials or money → not a nuisance. Tell Tier 3 now.
How many mailboxes got it? Search by sender AND subject AND URL.
Wide radius → P1, start the purge.
Did anybody click or submit?
Yes → §5 immediately, and GOV-03 incident.
Is the sender one of ours?
Yes → that account is compromised. Disable sign-in now, notice within the hour.
Purge tenant-wide, block sender and URLs, check for variants.
Record what was purged and when.
Does the community need telling?
§6. Notice from the established IT address, no links, no requested action.

appendices.head: Appendix B — End-user text
rows: If a message looks wrong
Use the Report button in Outlook. That sends us everything we need. Please don’t forward it — a forward loses the technical detail and puts another copy of it in a mailbox.
Not sure?
Report it anyway. It takes us two minutes to check and nobody has ever been made to feel silly for asking.
Already clicked?
Tell us straight away. This is the single most helpful thing you can do, and you will not be in trouble. What we can fix in ten minutes is much harder to fix the next day.
Please don’t warn colleagues by forwarding it
It spreads the message. Tell us and we will tell everyone at once.
We will never ask for your password or a code
Not by email, not on the phone, not in a ticket. If someone does, they are not IT.

title: Loaner Device Issue, Support & Return
subtitle: The two-minute check before a loaner goes out, and the ten minutes after it comes back.
tierText: Tier 1 — the Service Desk, which already holds the storage room. Faults escalate to Tier 2.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and at the start of each busy season.

callouts.title: If any check fails
lines: Do not issue the device. Take the next one, and put the failed one into Tier 2’s queue with a note of exactly what failed.
Issuing a device you know has a fault, with a caveat to the user, is how a pool earns a bad reputation. There is no version of “it mostly works” that helps somebody whose own machine has just died.

steps.text: Power on and sign in. Confirm it reaches a usable desktop without a pending update reboot queued.
steps.label: Power on and sign…

steps.text: Open Settings. This sounds trivial; a documented fault was precisely that Settings would not open, and it indicates a broken profile that will produce a cascade of other failures.
steps.label: Open Settings

steps.text: Open Teams, and confirm sign-in works. Teams is what most people need first and it is the commonest reported loaner fault.
steps.label: Open Teams, and confirm sign-in works

steps.text: Test the camera, the microphone and the speakers. Actually test them — play a sound, see the picture. A speaker fault discovered in a meeting is the exact case on record.
steps.label: Test the camera, the microphone…

steps.text: Confirm network: wired and wireless both, and VPN if the person will work remotely (DEV-10).
steps.label: Confirm network

steps.text: Confirm it is Intune-enrolled and compliant, and that BitLocker is on with the key escrowed (DEV-03 §5.1). A loaner passes DEV-01 exit criteria before every issue, not only at first build.
steps.label: Confirm it is Intune-enrolled and compliant…

steps.text: Confirm battery and charger. Send the charger; a loaner without one is half a loaner.
steps.label: Confirm battery and charger

steps.label: Record the check in the loaner…

steps.text: Record who has it, the asset tag, the date out, the expected return date, and the reason.
steps.label: Record who has it, the asset…

steps.text: Set an expected return date always. “Until my laptop is fixed” is not a date, and it is how a loaner becomes permanent.
steps.label: Set an expected return date always

steps.text: Explain what is on it and what is not: their files come from OneDrive and SharePoint, not from the loaner, and anything saved only to the loaner’s local disk will be wiped on return (M365-12).
steps.label: Explain what…

steps.text: Explain that it is an organization device under the same rules as any other — including the Acceptable Use standard (ACC-15) and that it may be remotely wiped if lost (DEV-16).
steps.label: Explain that it is an organization…

steps.text: Confirm they can sign in before they leave the desk. This one step prevents the majority of “the loaner doesn’t work” contacts.
steps.label: Confirm they can sign in before…

steps.text: Confirm the charger and any accessories came back.
steps.label: Confirm the charger and any accessories…

steps.text: Ask the person what did not work. Ask directly — people frequently do not report a fault on a device they are giving back, and this is the cheapest fault-finding available.
steps.label: Ask the person what did not…

steps.text: Check for data saved locally. Move anything institutional to the right place before wiping (M365-12).
steps.label: Check for data saved locally

steps.text: Confirm the BitLocker key is escrowed BEFORE wiping (DEV-03 §8).
steps.label: Confirm the BitLocker key is escrowed…

steps.text: Wipe and re-provision via Autopilot. A returned loaner goes back to a known-good state rather than to whatever state the last user left it in.
steps.label: Wipe and re-provision via Autopilot

steps.text: Run the full §3 pre-issue check and record the result. The device is not back in the pool until it passes.
steps.label: Run the full pre-issue check…

steps.text: Note any fault found in the loaner log against that asset tag. Faults recurring on the same tag are §7.
steps.label: Note any fault found…

steps.text: Clear the primary user in inventory so the device shows as available (DEV-01 §10).
steps.label: Clear the primary user in inventory…

title: Legacy File Share Retirement & Migration Runbook
subtitle: How legacy network drives are retired without losing content, scattering it into personal OneDrives, or breaking payroll access on the way.

steps.label: List every top-level share on the…

steps.text: For each share, identify a departmental owner — a named person, not a department. Where nobody can be found, that share goes to §6.
steps.label: For each share, identify a departmental…

steps.label: Classify each share with its owner…

steps.label: Record the current access

steps.label: Flag anything with a last-modified date…

steps.label: Create the destination site under M365-10…

steps.label: Agree with the owner what…

steps.text: Run both in parallel for at least one full working week. The source is still authoritative during this period and people are told so.

title: Microsoft 365 Service Description & Supported Baseline
subtitle: What the organization provides, what it does not, and which configurations IT can actually help with. The document every other M365 procedure points back to.

appendices.head: Appendix A — Staff FAQ
rows: What email do I get?
A full Exchange Online mailbox with an address at your domain, reachable from Outlook on your computer, at outlook.office.com, and on your phone.
Can I read organization email on my own phone?
Yes. We apply protection to the organization apps only — see DEV-07 for exactly what we can and cannot see, which is much less than people assume.
Where should I save my files?
Your own drafts and working notes: OneDrive. Anything your department relies on, or that the organization would need if you left: your department’s SharePoint site.
Do I need the VPN?
Almost certainly not. Email, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive all work from anywhere. The VPN is only for on-premises systems (DEV-10).
I forgot my password
aka.ms/sspr resets it without contacting anyone, provided you have two security methods registered. Registering the second one takes two minutes and is the best five minutes you will spend.
I have a new phone
Set up your security method on the new phone BEFORE you get rid of the old one. Otherwise you will need to verify your identity in person or on video with photo ID.
Which browser should I use?
Current Edge, Chrome, Firefox or Safari. All fine.
Can I use a different mail app?
Outlook is what we support. Others may work, but we will not be able to help much when they do not.
How do I get a shared departmental mailbox?
Ask the service desk. It needs a named owner from your department who approves who can read it (M365-03).
How do I email everyone in a group?
Through the office that owns that population — usually HR or Communications (M365-06).
How do I get a SharePoint site?
Ask the service desk with a named owner, a one-sentence purpose, and who needs access (M365-10).
Something is broken. Who do I ask?
The service desk. If it turns out not to be ours, we will send it to the right desk.
I think somebody else has been in my account
Tell the service desk straight away and say so explicitly. Do not change your password first — we need to see the sign-in trail before it changes.
Will IT ever ask for my password?
Never. Not by email, phone or ticket. Anyone who does is not IT.

appendices.head: Appendix A — The short version, for publication
rows: Your account is yours
Please do not give anybody your password, approve a login prompt you did not trigger, or let somebody else use your account. Not family, not friends, not colleagues, not in an emergency.
Do not use somebody else’s
Even if they said it was fine. Everything done with an account is, on the record, done by the person it belongs to.
Why it matters more than it sounds

Multifactor authentication, audit logs and account recovery all assume one account, one person. Sharing does not weaken one protection — it removes the ground the others stand on. And it leaves you answering for whatever happens next.
If you need shared access, ask

The organization has proper ways to do it — a shared mailbox, a shared site, a role group. They all keep working when somebody is away, and they record who did what. Ask the service desk; it usually takes a day.
VPNs and remote access
Do not use a VPN or proxy to disguise where you are signing in from, or to let somebody else appear to be you. Staff who need remote access have a supported way to get it.
We will never ask for your password
Not by email, not on the phone, not in a ticket. Anybody who does is not IT — please report it.
We will ask you to prove who you are
Before we change anything on your account. It takes about ninety seconds and it is the same check that stops somebody else doing it to your account.
If something has gone wrong

Tell us. If you shared a password, or clicked something, or let somebody use your account — telling us early is the single most helpful thing you can do, and it is a much smaller problem on the day than it is a week later.

title: Personally-Owned Device Access Standard
subtitle: What your own phone or laptop may reach, what the organization can and cannot see on it, and what happens when you leave.
tierText: Tier 4 — IT Management owns the position; Tier 2 supports it.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend Head of IT, with HR on §6 ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually.

appendices.head: Appendix A — End-user text
rows: Using your own phone for work email
Perfectly fine, and most people do. We apply protection to the organization apps — a passcode to open them, and a rule that organization files cannot be copied into personal apps.
What we can see
That the device exists, its model and OS version, and that organization apps are protected. That is all. Not your photos, messages, browsing, other apps or location.
What we can remove
Organization data from organization apps. We cannot wipe your device, and we would not.
What not to put on it

Do not download client records, job applicant files or personnel records to a personal device. Read them in the app instead. Never anything with social security numbers, card details or health information.
Your Authenticator phone
Keep a passcode on it, register a second method on something else, and set up the new phone BEFORE you get rid of the old one. That last one saves you a trip to the service desk with photo ID.
When you leave
We remove organization data from organization apps. Nothing else on your device is touched.
If you would rather not
Then do not — use an organization device, or just do organization work at work. There is no expectation and no consequence.

flows.head: 4. Mail: shared mailboxes and inactive mailboxes

callouts.title: Verify this once, on a test account, before the first separation is processed under the floor
lines: Create a test mailbox with known content. Convert it. Remove the licence. Wait a week. Confirm the content is still there and still searchable. Record the result as a permanent project record (M365-20 §9).
This is a Tier 3 task and a prerequisite to publishing ACC-01 (ACC-01 §9.2). It takes an afternoon and it is the difference between a policy and a hope.

steps.sub: 4.2 Shared mailbox conversion — the four conditions
steps.text: Confirm the mailbox is under 50 GB. An unlicensed shared mailbox is capped at 50 GB. Above that, or where an in-place archive or litigation hold is required on it, an Exchange Online Plan 2 licence must remain assigned — and that is a cost decision under M365-20, not a technical detail to be discovered afterwards.
steps.label: Confirm the mailbox is under 50…

steps.sub: 4.2 Shared mailbox conversion — the four conditions
steps.text: RESET THE PASSWORD and confirm sign-in is blocked. Microsoft is explicit: if the password is not reset, the original username and password continue to work on the shared mailbox after conversion. A converted mailbox still answering to the leaver’s old credentials is not offboarded, it is a shared credential with a forwarding address.
steps.label: RESET THE PASSWORD and confirm…

steps.sub: 4.2 Shared mailbox conversion — the four conditions
steps.text: Do not delete the user account. The account object anchors the shared mailbox. Deleting it destroys what it anchors. Disable; never delete (ACC-01 §7.2).
steps.label: Do not delete the user account

steps.sub: 4.2 Shared mailbox conversion — the four conditions
steps.text: IF THE ORGANIZATION IS IN EXCHANGE HYBRID: run Set-RemoteMailbox -Identity <identity> -Type Shared on-premises as well. Converting only in Exchange Online causes directory synchronisation to revert the mailbox to a regular mailbox, which then disconnects. Microsoft states that permanent loss of the mailbox contents can occur if these steps are not completed within 30 days. Whether the organization is still in hybrid at the time of any given separation is a question Tier 3 answers before the conversion, not after.
steps.label: THE ORGANIZATION IS IN EXCHANGE HYBRID: run?

steps.sub: 4.3 Inactive mailboxes — the sequence that matters
steps.text: Apply the hold FIRST. A Microsoft 365 retention policy configured to retain, or to retain and then delete, is the recommended mechanism. A delete-only policy is not a hold and will not preserve anything.
steps.label: Apply the hold FIRST

steps.sub: 4.3 Inactive mailboxes — the sequence that matters
steps.text: Confirm the hold is applied and reporting. Do not proceed on the basis that the policy exists somewhere in the tenant; confirm it covers this mailbox.
steps.label: Confirm the hold is applied…

steps.sub: 4.3 Inactive mailboxes — the sequence that matters
steps.text: Only then remove the licence. If the licence is removed from a mailbox before the hold is in place, the mailbox is no longer searchable — which means it can no longer be placed on hold, found, or exported. This failure is silent and irreversible.
steps.label: Only then remove the licence

steps.sub: 4.3 Inactive mailboxes — the sequence that matters
steps.text: An in-place archive attached to the mailbox is disabled immediately on licence removal, with a 30-day grace period. Where the archive holds content that matters, either the licence stays or the archive content is dealt with before reclamation.
steps.label: An in-place archive attached…

flows.head: 5. Ownership — a Form owned by a person dies with the person

callouts.title: The rule
lines: Any Form that supports an organization process — anything a department depends on, anything collecting data that will be kept, anything published beyond the person who built it — is created as a GROUP form, owned by a Microsoft 365 group.

This is one extra click at the moment of creation and it is the entire control. A group form can be handed on, reviewed, and found by somebody other than its author. A personal form can be transferred only by its owner, and only while they still have an account — which is to say, only before the moment you need it.

callouts.title: Open question — the forms nobody knows exist
lines: IT cannot currently produce a list of every Form in the tenant with its owner. Administrative reporting for Forms is thin, and this document is honest that §5 is therefore enforced at the moment of creation and by convention, not by audit.

ACTION: Tier 3 to establish what reporting is available — group forms are discoverable through the groups that own them, personal forms largely are not — and report to Tier 4 within 90 days of approval. If nothing useful exists, say so, and rely on §5 and the leaver checklist rather than claiming a control the organization does not have. Owner: Tier 3, reporting to the Head of IT.

steps.text: Create it in the group. In Forms, choose a new group form and pick the department’s group rather than accepting the default of your own account.
steps.label: Create it in the group

steps.text: If it already exists as a personal form, move it now, while you still can. Forms supports transferring a form to a group. Doing this today takes two minutes; doing it after somebody has left is not possible.
steps.label: It already exists as a personal form?

gate.cond: it already exists as a personal form
gate.then: move it now, while you still can

steps.text: Personal forms remain entirely appropriate for personal things — a straw poll in a meeting, a lunch order, a quick check with four colleagues. The test is whether anybody but you would miss it.
steps.label: Personal forms remain entirely appropriate…

steps.text: The group owner is accountable for what it collects (§3), who can read the responses (§7), and closing it when the thing it was for has finished. An open form collecting responses nobody reads is a data holding with no purpose.
steps.label: The group owner is accountable…

flows.head: 9. Bookings must not write into the ticket queue

callouts.title: The rule
lines: A Bookings page does not write into the ticketing system. No confirmation, reminder, cancellation, reschedule notice or staff notification from a Bookings page is addressed to the service desk address, or to any other address that creates a ticket.
This applies to pages owned by IT as well. Especially to pages owned by IT.

callouts.title: And the figures will not reconcile — which is the argument, not an aside
lines: Categories counted by heuristic rarely add back up to the total. A few dozen rows end up in two categories, or in the manual-review pile, or are caught by a filter applied at a different point.

Nobody does anything wrong, and the gap is usually small. The problem is that it cannot be resolved without going back to the raw export and repeating the work, because the queue itself does not distinguish an appointment from a ticket. A queue that has to be reconstructed to be counted cannot produce a baseline anybody should build an SLA on (GOV-06).
That is why this is a rule and not a suggestion.

steps.text: Bookings notifications are addressed to a departmental shared mailbox (M365-03) or to the assigned staff member. Never to an intake address.
steps.label: Bookings notifications are addressed…

steps.text: Tier 3 audits every existing Bookings page in the tenant for notification addresses that reach the service desk queue, and corrects them. OWNER: Tier 3. DUE: within 30 days of approval. This is a finite task with a known end.
steps.label: Tier 3 audits every existing Bookings…

steps.text: Where a booking genuinely should create a ticket — an IT appointment that ought to be tracked and closed — that is designed deliberately under GOV-02 with its own ticket category and its own queue treatment, not produced as a side effect of a confirmation email nobody chose.
steps.label: A booking genuinely should create a ticket?

steps.text: Appointments that must remain visible in the ticketing system for a legitimate reason are categorised so that they can be excluded from ticket counts at source. Excluding them at source is better than excluding them in the report, because a report is written by one person once and the queue is read by everybody forever.
steps.label: Appointments that must remain visible…

steps.text: GOV-02 owns the categorisation. This document owns the rule that produces the need for it.
steps.label: GOV-02 owns the categorisation

appendices.head: Appendix B — For end users: the plain version
rows: Build it in your group, not in your own account

When you create a Form, choose your department’s group rather than accepting the default. It takes one extra click. A form built in your personal account belongs to your account, and if you change role or leave, it goes with you — along with every response in it. Nobody gets a warning; it just stops being anybody’s. If you have already built one that your department relies on, move it into the group today. You can do that yourself, and you can only do it while you still have the account.
People outside the organization cannot upload files to a Form

This one catches everybody. Microsoft Forms cannot accept a file from somebody who does not have an organization account, because the file has to be saved into our own storage and they have nowhere to save it to. It is not a setting and it is not something IT can turn on. If you need a document from a job applicant, a customer or a vendor, ask the service desk — we will set up a folder they can upload into, or a mailbox they can email.
Three things never go in a Form

Social Security numbers, card details, and anything medical. Not even the last four digits of an SSN, and not even “just for this one event”. If somebody has asked you to collect one of these, that is exactly the moment to ask us — there is nearly always a proper route, and it is usually quicker than the workaround.
“Anonymous” means something specific

If you promise anonymity, set the form so it does not record names — and then be careful what else you ask. In a team of six, asking for department, role and length of service is asking for their name. And it stays anonymous: if somebody tells you something worrying, there is no way for anyone, including us, to find out who they were.
The responses are a real record

They live in a spreadsheet in your group’s site, and anyone who can get into that site can read them. If you export to Excel, that copy is out of our reach — please keep it in the department’s site. And when the thing is finished, close the form rather than deleting it, unless you are sure nobody needs what is in it.
Use Bookings for appointments, not a Form

A Form cannot hold a slot or stop two people booking the same time, so people end up sorting out clashes by hand. Bookings does all of that, sends the reminders, and handles cancellations. Ask us for a page and we will set it up with your business hours and a sensible amount of notice.
Tell colleagues before you add them to a booking page

Adding somebody as staff makes them bookable and connects the page to their calendar. That is a real change to someone’s day and it should be a conversation first. And if a slot looks free in their calendar the page will offer it, so set proper business hours rather than relying on the calendar being complete.
Booking confirmations must not go to the service desk

Please do not put the service desk address on a Bookings page. Every confirmation becomes a ticket, and when anyone tries to count the real tickets, separating out the appointments takes days. Send confirmations to your departmental mailbox instead — and if you are not sure which address that is, or whether a Form is the right tool at all, just ask. There is no ticket needed and nobody minds being asked.

title: Generative AI & Copilot Use in Microsoft 365
subtitle: What organization data may be put into which assistant — and why deploying Copilot across a tenant whose sharing has never been reviewed is how an organization discovers what it had been over-sharing.
tierText: Tier 4 — IT Management owns this document and every decision in it. Tier 3 configures. Tier 1 and Tier 2 answer §3 from the table and escalate anything the table does not cover.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend executive leadership, with senior leadership on §6 ]
audience: Every member of staff, for §2, §3 and Appendix A. IT administrators for §5, §7 and §8. IT Leadership and executive leadership for §4, §5 and §11.
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Every six months for the first two years, then annually. This is the fastest-moving subject in the catalogue and an annual cycle is not sufficient. First review no later than six months after adoption.

callouts.title: Say this plainly to whoever asks for Copilot
lines: Copilot does not create over-permissioning. It makes over-permissioning VISIBLE and EXPLOITABLE. The exposure was there the whole time; what changes is that it is now one question away instead of one archaeology project away.

Deploying Copilot across a tenant whose sharing has never been reviewed is how an organization discovers what it had been over-sharing. That discovery happens either way. The only decision available is whether it happens during a permissions review that IT runs deliberately, or in a meeting where somebody reads out a number they should never have had.

appendices.head: Appendix A — For everyone: the one-paragraph version, and the five things not to paste
rows: 1. Anything about a named client or customer

Their account, their records, a complaint, an email they sent you, a difficult situation you are trying to word carefully. Especially that last one — “help me write a sensitive email about a client” is the most natural request in the world, and it is the one that puts the most into the box.
2. Anything about a named colleague’s employment
Pay, performance, a grievance, a health matter, a reference, a reorganisation that has not been announced. If you would not leave it on the printer, do not paste it.
3. Anything the organization has not decided yet
Draft budgets, draft policies, contract terms under negotiation, anything from a leadership paper. Unpublished is unpublished, whatever you are using it for.
4. Anything out of the HR system or another system of record
An export, a report, a screenshot, a list of IDs. If it came out of a system holding the organization’s records, it does not go into a tool outside the organization.
5. Any password, key or access link
Yours or anybody else’s, including in a block of configuration you are asking for help with. Assistants are very good at reading configuration and completely indifferent to what is in it.
And really the first one:
Anything you would not be comfortable seeing quoted back, with the organization’s name attached. That test catches most of what the five above catch, and a few things they do not.

owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
audience: IT administrators. Departmental builders are the population this document governs rather than its audience — §3, §7 and Appendix B are written for them and should be published separately.
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and on any change to the connector classification in §6.

flows.head: 4. The register — and building the first one

callouts.title: Open question — who actually keeps the register
lines: Often there is no Power Platform administrator role assigned. This document assumes one is named, and it should be named before §4 step 1 rather than after.

RECOMMENDATION: a named Tier 3 administrator holds it, with a nominated deputy. Not one keeper — a register maintained by exactly one person is subject to precisely the failure mode described in §1, which would be an unusually poor joke to build into the control.
ACTION: Head of IT to name the role and the deputy at approval. Owner: Head of IT.

steps.text: Tier 3 produces an inventory of every flow and app in the tenant from the Power Platform admin centre: name, owner, environment, connectors used, last run, and run failure count. This is an export and a morning’s work, not a project. OWNER: Tier 3. DUE: within 30 days of approval.
steps.label: Tier 3 produces an inventory…

steps.text: Triage first anything whose owner has already left, or whose connections are failing. Each one is dispositioned as still needed / stop it / rebuild it properly under §7. Expect this list to be longer than anybody predicts, and expect at least one item on it to matter.
steps.label: Triage first anything whose owner has…

steps.text: Everything remaining gets an owner confirmed in writing by the department, plus one line saying what it does and one saying what breaks if it stops. Two sentences per solution is the entire documentation requirement, and it is enough.
steps.label: It stops?

gate.cond: it stops. Two sentences per solution is the entire documentation requirement
gate.then: and it is enough

steps.text: Publish the register back to the departments, by department. This is what makes it useful to them rather than an audit imposed on them, and a department reading its own list will reliably find one it had forgotten about. That is the register earning its keep on day one.
steps.label: Publish the register back…

steps.text: From then on, registration happens at build time via Appendix A, and Tier 3 reconciles the register against a fresh admin-centre export quarterly (§10). A register maintained only by self-declaration decays quietly; one reconciled against the platform does not.
steps.label: From then on, registration happens…

steps.text: Cross-check the register against ACC-01 §7.2 at every separation: does this person own a registered flow, app or connection? The register is what turns that from an unanswerable question into a thirty-second lookup.
steps.label: Cross-check the register against the leaver list…

flows.name: The register — and building the first one

flows.head: 9. When a departmental solution has become an application

steps.text: Either the department raises it, or IT raises it from the quarterly register reconciliation (§10). Raising it is not a criticism of the person who built it — in most cases it is a compliment about how useful the thing turned out to be, and it is worth saying so.
steps.label: Either the department raises it…

steps.text: It goes through ACC-16 application onboarding: what it does, what it touches, who owns it, how it authenticates, what happens when it fails, and who is called when it does.
steps.label: It goes through ACC-16 application onboarding

steps.text: IT decides one of three outcomes, and says which: ADOPT — IT takes ownership, moves it to the production environment, and supports it under GOV-04 change control. SUPPORT IN PLACE — it stays with the department, IT has documented it and monitors it, and the department knows what it is responsible for. RETIRE AND REPLACE — it is doing something an existing supported system already does, and the right answer is to stop maintaining a second one.
steps.label: IT decides one of three outcomes…

steps.text: “Adopt” is a real commitment and it is made deliberately, against the capacity to honour it. An IT department that adopts every departmental flow and then cannot maintain them has made the situation worse, not better, and has taken the department’s ownership away in exchange for nothing. It is honest and better to say: we are not adopting this, here is what you must do to keep running it safely, and here is what we will help with.
steps.label: “Adopt” is a real commitment…

steps.text: Once adopted, it is under GOV-04 from that day. Changes are changes, they go in a window, and they have a rollback. That is the trade the department gets in exchange for handing it over, and it is worth being explicit that the flexibility they had is part of what they are giving up.
steps.label: It is under GOV-04…

title: Service, Application & Non-Human Account Standard
subtitle: The identities that are not people — which kind to use, who owns them, how their credentials are held and rotated, and how they end.
tierText: Tier 3 — Expert Services creates, holds and reviews every non-human identity. Tier 4 approves any privileged assignment and every multifactor exemption. Tier 1 and Tier 2 act on this document only by refusing an interactive sign-in request and escalating it.
