callouts.title: An expired secret takes an integration down at three in the morning, and the symptom never says so.
lines: What appears is “the overnight HR feed did not run”, or “nobody can sign in to the portal”, or a queue quietly filling up that somebody notices on Tuesday. Hours are then spent rediscovering a fact that was knowable months in advance and written on a certificate.

So expiries are TRACKED, not discovered. Every credential expiry date is entered in the register at the moment the credential is issued — not later, not when somebody gets round to it. A credential issued without its expiry recorded is a future outage that has already been scheduled.

steps.sub: 6.3 Expiry monitoring — the part that actually matters
steps.text: The expiry date is recorded in the register at issue, by the person who issued it.
steps.label: The expiry date is recorded…

steps.sub: 6.3 Expiry monitoring — the part that actually matters
steps.text: Tier 3 produces a monthly report of every credential expiring within 90 days, and takes it to Tier 4 as a standing item.
steps.label: Tier 3 produces a monthly report…

steps.sub: 6.3 Expiry monitoring — the part that actually matters
steps.text: The owner and the deputy are notified at 60, 30 and 7 days. Notices go to people, not to a shared mailbox that nobody has been made responsible for reading.
steps.label: The owner and the deputy…

steps.sub: 6.3 Expiry monitoring — the part that actually matters
steps.text: Rotate with overlap wherever the platform allows two credentials: add the new one, confirm the integration is using it, then remove the old one. An application registration supports this; a password does not, which is one more reason §3 prefers the former.
steps.label: Rotate with overlap wherever the platform…

steps.sub: 6.3 Expiry monitoring — the part that actually matters
steps.text: Record the rotation and the new expiry in the register. A rotation that is not recorded has reset the clock on a date nobody knows.
steps.label: Record the rotation and the new…

steps.sub: 6.3 Expiry monitoring — the part that actually matters
steps.text: An expiry that arrives with no rotation ticket already open is a defect in this procedure and is reported as one under GOV-01, not treated as bad luck.
steps.label: An expiry that arrives with no…

steps.text: The HR leaver notification (ACC-01 §5.1) triggers a register query: which non-human accounts does this person own or deputise for?
steps.label: The HR leaver notification…

steps.text: Ownership transfers before the last working day. The deputy becomes the owner, or the leaver’s manager names a replacement. This is part of the handover conversation, not an IT afterthought.
steps.label: Ownership transfers before the last working…

steps.text: Every credential the leaver held or could retrieve is rotated at separation. Without exception, and regardless of how the departure went — this is not a statement about the person. It is what makes it possible to say, in a year, that the credential was not available to anybody outside the organization.
steps.label: Every credential the leaver held…

steps.text: Shared operational account passwords are changed on the departure of anyone who knew them (§6.2).
steps.label: Shared operational account passwords are changed…

steps.text: Where no owner can be found, the account is escalated to Tier 4 with a 30-day disable date. The burden of proof sits on keeping it, not on removing it.
steps.label: No owner can be found?

gate.cond: no owner can be found
gate.then: the account is escalated to Tier 4 with a 30-day disable date

steps.text: Where the leaver is themselves a vendor or contractor, ACC-11 §10 runs as well; the account may be one the organization created for them, and the contract end date may already have passed.
steps.label: The leaver is themselves a vendor?

gate.cond: the leaver is themselves a vendor or contractor
gate.then: ACC-11 §10 runs as well

callouts.title: The rule that unblocks this section
lines: A non-human account that nobody can explain is decommissioned, not researched indefinitely. If disabling it breaks something, the thing it broke will announce itself within a fortnight and the account can be re-enabled in minutes.

That is a considerably cheaper way of establishing what an account does than an archaeology project, and it is the only approach that ever actually reduces the population. The alternative — leaving it because somebody might need it — is how the organization arrives at an estate nobody can account for.
Do it deliberately: disable in a maintenance window under GOV-04, tell Tier 2 and Tier 3 what has been disabled and why, and be ready to reverse it the same day.

steps.text: DISABLE first. Never delete as the first action — deletion removes the evidence of what the account was and, for a service principal, takes its permission grants with it.
steps.label: DISABLE first

steps.text: Observe for 30 days. Watch for the failures that tell you what it was doing.
steps.label: Observe for 30 days

steps.text: Remove its permissions and group memberships, recording what they were before removal.
steps.label: Remove its permissions and group memberships…

steps.text: Revoke and remove its credentials.
steps.label: Revoke and remove its credentials

steps.text: Delete the object, and record the deletion in the register with the date and the approver. A deleted application registration is recoverable for a limited window; a deleted on-premises account is not, unless it is in a backup somebody can find.
steps.label: Delete the object, and record…

steps.text: Close the register entry rather than deleting the row. The history of what existed is worth more than a tidy list.
steps.label: Close the register entry rather than…

title: Vendor, Contractor & Consultant Account Standard
subtitle: The account class for people who work with the organization but not for it — the sponsor, the expiry that is not negotiable, and the day the relationship quietly changes.
tierText: Tier 3 — Expert Services holds vendor identities and all vendor privileged access. Tier 4 approves standing privileged access and every exception. Tier 2 creates and ends the routine contractor account.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend Head of IT, with Procurement on §8 ]

flows.head: 5. When the relationship changes — conversion in both directions

callouts.title: A class change is a re-baseline, never a continuation.
lines: If entitlements are carried across a class change, the person accumulates the union of every role they have ever held — which is how a former Finance administrator ends up as a consultant with standing access to payroll-sensitive material that nobody granted deliberately.

This will occasionally feel discourteous, and it is worth saying so to the person rather than letting them discover it. The framing that works is honest: the organization is not withdrawing trust, it is matching access to the current engagement, and anything genuinely needed is granted the same week on the sponsor’s request.
The alternative framing — quietly leaving the old access in place because it would be awkward to remove — is the one that has to be defended later, and it cannot be.

steps.text: The full leaver procedure runs (ACC-01 §7.2). Sessions revoked, entitlements removed, disposition set under ACC-12. This happens even though the person is coming back on Monday.
steps.label: The full leaver procedure runs (ACC-01…

steps.text: A new account is created under this document, with a sponsor and a contract-end expiry.
steps.label: A new account is created…

steps.text: Entitlements are granted from zero against the contracted work — not carried over, and not restored from a list of what they used to have.
steps.label: Entitlements are granted from zero…

steps.text: Any privileged access is re-approved by Tier 4 as a new grant (ACC-07). Previous seniority is not an entitlement.
steps.label: Any privileged access is re-approved…

steps.text: The class change is recorded (Appendix B), including what was removed. The record is what makes the following year’s review meaningful.
steps.label: The class change is recorded (Appendix…

flows.name: When the relationship changes — conversion in both directions

callouts.title: Contract end is rarely a clean event, and the procedure should assume it is not
lines: A support agreement lapses and is renewed six weeks later. A project “finishes” but the vendor is still answering questions months later. An engineer leaves the vendor and nobody thinks to say so.

The expiry date handles all three correctly: the account expires, and a renewal takes one email from the sponsor. The failure mode this prevents is the account staying live across a gap that nobody is tracking — which is not a theoretical risk, it is what happens by default.

steps.text: The sponsor notifies IT at contract or engagement end. Where they do not, the expiry set under §4 catches it — which is the entire purpose of §4.
steps.label: The sponsor notifies IT at contract…

steps.text: Disable the accounts; do not delete them. Deleting destroys the record of what the vendor held, which is exactly what is wanted six months later.
steps.label: Disable the accounts

steps.text: Revoke sessions and tokens, and remove VPN and remote access profiles (DEV-10).
steps.label: Revoke sessions and tokens, and remove…

steps.text: ROTATE EVERY CREDENTIAL THE VENDOR HELD OR COULD RETRIEVE — shared appliance and console passwords, any service account they were given, any certificate or secret they installed (ACC-08 §6, §10). This is not a comment on the vendor. It is what makes it possible to state, afterwards, that the credential is no longer outside the organization.
steps.label: ROTATE EVERY CREDENTIAL THE VENDOR HELD…

steps.text: Remove them from privileged groups and record what was removed before removing it.
steps.label: Remove them from privileged groups…

steps.text: Confirm in writing that organization data held in the vendor’s own systems has been returned or destroyed, per §8. The account ending does not reach their laptop, their ticketing system or their backups, and this is the only mechanism that does.
steps.label: Confirm in writing that organization data…

steps.text: Close the register entry with the date, and note any non-human account created for the integration so it goes through ACC-08 §11 rather than being left running.
steps.label: Close the register entry…

steps.text: Where the vendor relationship ended badly, treat it as an immediate separation: same-hour disable, credential rotation first, and Tier 4 informed (GOV-03 if there is any suspicion of misuse).
steps.label: The vendor relationship ended badly?

title: Account Suspension for Misuse or Policy Investigation
subtitle: IT contains. The department head, HR or senior leadership sanctions. What the organization suspends, on what basis, what it hands over, and what the person is told.
tierText: Tier 4 — IT Management authorises every suspension beyond immediate containment, and owns every referral. Tier 3 executes and assembles the evidence. Tier 1 and Tier 2 contain and escalate; they do not suspend and they do not refer.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]

callouts.title: Containment has a clock, and somebody has to be watching it.
lines: A containment block still in place after FIVE COVERAGE DAYS without either restoration or a Tier 4 decision to hold it is escalated to Tier 4 automatically, by whoever notices, without waiting to be asked.

Containment that has quietly become indefinite is a sanction that nobody decided to impose. It has all the effect of a suspension and none of the process, and it usually happens not through any intent but because the ticket moved down the queue.
In a small, stretched team, tickets do move down queues. That is precisely why this one carries an automatic escalation rather than relying on somebody remembering.

steps.text: PRESERVE FIRST. Capture the sign-in records, the multifactor registration history and the relevant audit data before remediating. Once sessions are revoked and credentials changed, the trail is materially harder to reconstruct, and it is the trail that later decides whether this was sharing, compromise or nothing (GOV-03 §6).
steps.label: PRESERVE FIRST

steps.text: Block sign-in and revoke sessions and tokens.
steps.label: Block sign-in and revoke sessions…

steps.text: Force a password reset and remove all multifactor methods for re-registration (ACC-03 §9).
steps.label: Force a password reset and remove…

steps.text: Record the technical basis in one sentence, in neutral terms — what was observed, not what it is thought to mean (§5).
steps.label: Record the technical basis in one…

steps.text: Notify the person promptly, through a channel independent of the suspended account (§8). This is a step in the procedure, not a courtesy to be fitted in later.
steps.label: Notify the person promptly, through…

steps.text: Escalate to Tier 4 if the block will be held beyond the technical need, or if any referral is contemplated.
steps.label: The block will be held beyond?

gate.cond: the block will be held beyond the technical need

steps.text: Where several accounts share the same indicators — open ONE investigation, not several tickets, and notify Tier 3 (ACC-03 §10). Splitting a single pattern across six tickets is how it stops looking like a pattern.
steps.label: Several accounts share the same indicators —?

gate.cond: several accounts share the same indicators — open ONE investigation

title: Application Onboarding, SSO & SAML Claims Standard
subtitle: What IT needs before an application is federated, which protocol it gets, the claim set every application receives — and how an application moves from one identity provider to another without breaking on the day.
tierText: Tier 3 — Expert Services owns federation, claim configuration and the identity provider. Tier 4 approves every cutover of an application already in use. Tier 1 and Tier 2 do not configure federation, and should not be asked to.

flows.head: 5. NameID — immutable, non-reassignable, and never an email address

callouts.title: The rule, and it is not a preference
lines: NameID is the value the application uses to decide which existing user this is. It must be immutable — it never changes for a given person — and non-reassignable — it is never later given to somebody else.
An email address is neither. Changing an address is a routine, supported, correct workflow with its own procedure (M365-05).
So: NameID is user.objectid, in persistent format, on every new integration. No exceptions without a Tier 4 decision recorded on the register.

steps.text: Identify them. For each federated application, record the NameID source attribute and format on the register. Where it is an email address or a UPN, flag it.
steps.label: Identify them

steps.text: Add every flagged application to the M365-05 procedure as a named downstream dependency, so that an address change triggers a per-application remediation instead of a surprise. This is a small edit to M365-05 and it is the immediate mitigation.
steps.label: Add every flagged application…

steps.text: Migrate the identifier at the next cutover (§8). That is the natural moment, because the trust relationship is being rebuilt anyway and the vendor is already engaged.
steps.label: Migrate the identifier at the next…

steps.text: Be realistic about the cost. Changing the NameID on a live application means the vendor must re-map every existing user record from the old value to the new one. Some vendors do this on request, some charge for it, and some cannot do it at all — in which case the application stays flagged, permanently, and that fact belongs in the annual report to Tier 4 rather than in an engineer’s memory.
steps.label: Be realistic about the cost

flows.head: 8. Current state, target state, and migrating an application

callouts.title: The rollback question that must be answered before, not after
lines: Establish, in writing from the vendor, what the application does when the identifier changes. Some applications rebind an existing record to the new NameID on first sign-in; some create a duplicate; some refuse the sign-in outright.

This matters because it determines whether the rollback still works. If the application has already rebound its records to the new identifier, restoring the old identity provider does not restore the old state — the users are now keyed to a value the old provider does not send, and the rollback fails silently at the second step.

Where the vendor cannot answer this question, the answer is found on a test instance before the cutover is scheduled. Where there is no test instance, the change is escalated as irreversible under GOV-04 §5.

steps.text: RECORD THE CURRENT STATE COMPLETELY BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING: the existing NameID source attribute and format, every claim and its exact name, the group or role mapping, the provisioning configuration, the signing certificate and its expiry, and the list of users who actually sign in. A rollback to a configuration nobody wrote down is a reconstruction, not a rollback.
steps.label: Record the current state completely…

steps.text: Build the target configuration in Entra against §4, §5 and §6. Where the current NameID is an email address, this is the moment §5.2 is paid for, and the vendor conversation about re-mapping existing records happens now — not on the night.
steps.label: Build the target configuration in…

steps.text: Where the application supports more than one federation connection, configure both and run them in parallel — it converts the cutover from an event into a switch, and is worth asking for even when it is not offered. Where it supports only one, the cutover is atomic and the rollback is the restoration of the old provider’s connection: TESTED, with the metadata, certificate and claim mapping held ready and confirmed still valid, not assumed to be a matter of pasting a URL back.
steps.label: Run both connections in parallel where…

steps.text: Pilot with named real users drawn from every population that uses the application: one who is not in IT, one on a personal or unmanaged device (DEV-07), one temporary worker on a second account, and one person who is in a great many groups (§6).
steps.label: Pilot with named real users drawn…

steps.text: Run the pilot for a stated period with a named contact and a stated back-out trigger — the specific observation that ends the pilot rather than a general sense that it is going badly.
steps.label: Run the pilot for a stated…

steps.text: Cut over inside a maintenance window under GOV-04, with a change record, a named organization approver, and a communication that tells people what to do if it does not work for them.
steps.label: Cut over inside a maintenance window…

steps.text: Verify with a real sign-in from each population before the window closes. The engineer’s own account is not a verification (§4.1). Keep the source configuration in place but disabled for 30 days — deleting the rollback path on the night converts a five-minute recovery into a rebuild under pressure.
steps.label: Verify with a real…

steps.text: Record the cutover under GOV-04 and update the register: migration state, new claim mapping, the Appendix B worksheet, and anything the vendor did on their side.
steps.label: Record the cutover under GOV-04…

title: Periodic Access Review & Entitlement Recertification
subtitle: Without recertification, every grant becomes permanent by default. What is reviewed, on what cycle, by whom — and what actually happens when nobody answers.
tierText: Tier 4 — IT Management owns the cycle and receives the annual report. Tier 3 produces the lists; Tier 2 executes the removals. No tier of IT decides whether a person still needs access.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend Head of IT, with executive leadership on §5 ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and after the first full cycle has run once.

flows.head: 3. Who reviews — and why it is never IT

callouts.title: The counter-argument, and why it does not change the answer
lines: Managers do not want to do this. It takes time they do not have, it is not their job as they understand it, and asking them is unpopular. All of that is true and none of it is a reason to move the decision.

The alternative fails in both directions. If IT removes access on its own judgement, it will eventually remove something somebody needed, and the department will stop co-operating with the process entirely — which costs far more than the grant that was removed. If IT keeps everything to avoid that, the review is theatre and produces evidence of a control that is not operating, which is worse than having no control at all.
What IT can do is make it cheap. That is §4, and it is the part of this document that determines whether any of the rest of it happens.

steps.text: Produce the list — accurately, from the platform, for the whole class rather than the part that is easy to extract.
steps.label: Produce the list — accurately…

steps.text: Make it readable — §4. A list a department head can act on in ten minutes gets acted on; a list of object IDs gets approved wholesale.
steps.label: Make it readable

steps.text: Act on the answer, promptly and visibly. A reviewer who spends forty minutes on a review and sees nothing change will not do the next one, and there is no recovering from that. Removals are executed within the §6 service level and the reviewer is told they were done.
steps.label: Act on the answer, promptly…

flows.name: Who reviews — and why it is never IT

appendices.head: Appendix A — The reviewer’s one-page instruction sheet
rows: What this is

A list of the people who currently have access to something you are responsible for. We are asking you to confirm whether each of them should still have it. We are not suggesting anything is wrong — this is a routine check we run on a schedule.
Why we are asking you and not deciding ourselves

We can see who has access. We cannot see whether they still need it. Only you know whether that project finished, whether the cover arrangement is still running, or whether somebody has changed roles. If we guessed, we would either take away something you need or keep everything, and neither is any use to you.
What we need from you
For each line: Keep, Remove, or Change. If you choose Change, tell us in a few words what they should have instead. That is the whole task.
How long it takes
Most lists take about ten minutes. If yours is long enough that it does not, tell us — that usually means we have batched it wrongly and we will split it.
Four questions that make it quick
1. Do they still do the work this access was for? 2. If they asked you for it today, would you say yes? 3. Do they need this much, or would less do? 4. Do you recognise the name at all?
If you are not sure

Choose Remove. If it turns out somebody needed it, we will put it back the next working day, with no argument and no form to fill in. Keeping something “just in case” is exactly how these lists get longer every year.
If a name means nothing to you
Say so. An entitlement nobody can account for is one we should not be carrying, and telling us that is genuinely one of the most useful answers you can give.
If you are not the right person
Tell us who is, and we will send it to them and update our records. This is the single thing that will most reduce the time this takes you next time.
What happens next
We make the changes within five working days and tell you they are done. Your answers are kept, so next time we will send you only what has changed since — which usually takes about five minutes.
What happens if you do not reply

We will remind you at ten working days, and let your manager know at fifteen. At twenty working days we will tell you the date on which the access will be removed, and at twenty-five we remove it. We would much rather have your answer than do that.
If you need more time
Ask. A short extension recorded on the review is entirely normal, and it is far better than a rushed approval or a silence we have to escalate.
Who to ask
Reply to the message that sent you this list, or contact the service desk, quoting the review reference at the top of your packet.

title: IT Change Management & Maintenance Windows
subtitle: Three change classes, one register, an agreed set of windows the organization’s calendar governs — and the rule that a vendor change is an organization change.
tierText: Tier 4 — IT Management approves normal and emergency changes and owns the window and freeze calendar. Tier 3 assesses and executes. Tier 2 executes standard changes with no approval at all, which is the point of §3.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually — and the freeze calendar before each busy season begins, against the published calendar rather than last year’s copy.

callouts.title: A vendor change is an organization change.
lines: It enters the same register, with an organization approver, a back-out and a communication — whoever executes it, however routine it is, and however competent the vendor.

The vendor’s own change process is their internal control. It is not the organization’s record, and it is not visible to anybody at the organization three months later when something on that system behaves oddly.

This is the rule a real remediation teaches. Nothing in that kind of remediation is done badly. It is simply that the organization has no record of it, and could not have told the vendor “not that week” had the week been a peak week.

steps.text: The vendor’s request enters the register as a normal change, raised by the organization system or contract owner. It does not stay in the email thread it arrived in.
steps.label: The vendor’s request enters the register…

steps.text: The organization names an approver. The vendor is never the approver of a change to an organization system — not because their judgement is doubted, but because approval is an accountability the organization cannot outsource.
steps.label: The organization names an approver

steps.text: The record states what the vendor will do, on which systems, in which order, and what the back-out is. Test before Production is the correct sequence and it should be visible in the record, as it should be in any vendor thread. Where the vendor cannot supply a back-out, that is escalated under §5.2 rather than accepted as normal practice.
steps.label: The record states what the vendor…

steps.text: An organization engineer is available during the window — not necessarily executing, but reachable, and able to verify afterwards. A vendor change verified only by the vendor is a change nobody at the organization has confirmed.
steps.label: An organization engineer is available during…

steps.text: Verification is performed by the organization against a stated check, and recorded. “The vendor said it went fine” is not a verification.
steps.label: Verification is performed by the organization…

steps.text: STANDING vendor maintenance — a recurring patching cadence, for example — is approved ONCE as a standing change with a defined scope, a named window and a stated back-out, and each execution is then a one-line register entry (Appendix B, STD-12). This is the standard-change mechanism applied to vendors, and it is what stops the process being abandoned for the routine work it was never meant to obstruct.
steps.label: STANDING vendor maintenance — a recurring…

steps.text: The requirement to route changes through the organization register belongs in the vendor’s contract and in the operating agreement at renewal (ACC-11). Until it does, this section depends on goodwill — which is worth having, and is not a control.
steps.label: The requirement to route changes through…

callouts.title: The count is the finding, not the individual change
lines: A department with many emergency changes does not have an emergency problem. It has a planning problem, a fragility problem, or a vendor whose lead times do not fit the organization — and the register is the only instrument that makes the difference visible.
Emergency changes are counted monthly and reported annually. A rising count is a matter for Tier 4 to act on, not a fact about a difficult month.

steps.text: Obtain approval from Tier 4 before acting where a delay of minutes is available — verbally or by message. Where Tier 4 is unreachable, the Head of IT; where neither is reachable, the most senior person available, named on the record afterwards.
steps.label: Obtain approval from Tier 4 before…

steps.text: Act. Nothing in this section prevents an engineer from acting to protect or restore a service. Acting is correct; not recording it afterwards is what this section forbids.
steps.label: Act

steps.text: Write the record within one coverage day, including what back-out was available and whether it was used.
steps.label: Write the record within one coverage…

steps.text: Obtain and record retrospective approval within one coverage day.
steps.label: Obtain and record retrospective approval within…

steps.text: Hold a post-implementation review at the next monthly register review, for every emergency change, without exception (§11).
steps.label: Hold a post-implementation review…

flows.head: 11. Post-implementation review, and the monthly register review

callouts.title: How the process gets lighter instead of heavier
lines: The standard-change list grows by evidence. A normal change performed three times with the same outcome and no surprises is a candidate; Tier 4 adds it at the monthly review, with its conditions and its back-out stated.
That is the mechanism by which this document becomes cheaper to follow over time, which is the only way a process survives in a department this size.
The two failure signals are worth naming. A standard list that never grows means the process is not being used. A list that grows without evidence means it is being used to avoid the process.

steps.text: Did it do what it was meant to do?
steps.label: Did it do what it was?

steps.text: What did we not anticipate?
steps.label: What did we not anticipate??

steps.text: Was the back-out adequate — and if it was used, did it work within the time we said it would?
steps.label: It was used?

gate.cond: it was used
gate.then: did it work within the time we said it would?

steps.text: Did the communication reach the people who needed it, in time to be useful?
steps.label: Did the communication reach the people?

steps.text: Should this become a standard change — or should it never be attempted this way again?
steps.label: Should this become a standard change?

title: Standard Hardware Catalog, Request & Refresh Cycle
subtitle: What the organization buys, how you ask for it, how often it is replaced, and what it honestly costs in weeks.
tierText: Tier 4 — IT Management owns the catalogue, approves every off-catalogue exception and owns the annual refresh position. Tier 2 confirms technical fit and builds the device. Tier 1 answers “what will I get and when”.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend Head of IT, with the CFO on §8 ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: The document annually. The model annex in §3 twice a year, because vendor configurations change faster than SOPs do.

callouts.title: New joiners are the case this most often fails
lines: A device that arrives after somebody’s start date is the most visible failure in this whole document, and it is almost always caused by IT being told about the joiner in the same week they arrive.

Where HR owns onboarding intake and routing, A hardware request needs to leave HR at the offer-accepted point, not the week-of-arrival point, because §10 is three weeks in the good case. ACC-01 §5 is the intake; this document is what it triggers.

Where the lead time genuinely cannot be met, the answer is a loaner on day one with the real device to follow (DEV-05) — not an expedited purchase at a worse price, and not a first week with no computer.

steps.text: Requester or their manager raises a ticket stating: the person, their role, their start date if it is a new joiner, the catalogue class requested, and the bundle (§4). Not a model number, and not a link to a vendor page.
steps.label: Requester or their manager raises…

steps.text: Budget holder confirms funding in writing on the ticket. An email approval attached to the ticket is fine; a verbal one is not, because in six months nobody will remember it and the department will dispute the charge.
steps.label: Budget holder confirms funding in writing…

steps.text: Tier 2 confirms fit, and says so on the ticket in one line. Where a different class is the better answer, Tier 2 proposes it with the reason — an S4 desktop for a fixed desk, an S1 rather than an S3 for somebody who does not actually travel.
steps.label: Tier 2 confirms fit, and says…

steps.text: Where it is off-catalogue, §6 runs here. Where it is an S5 workstation, Tier 4 approves on the strength of the work.
steps.label: It is off-catalogue?

gate.cond: it is off-catalogue
gate.then: §6 runs here

steps.text: Order placed. The ticket records the order date and the expected delivery window from §10, and the requester is told that date rather than left to ask.
steps.label: Order placed

steps.text: On arrival: asset-tagged, recorded in inventory against the person and the cost centre, and enrolled per DEV-01. A device that reaches a desk without an inventory record is a device that will be missing from the §8 forecast and from every audit thereafter.
steps.label: On arrival

steps.text: Built to the DEV-02 baseline, encrypted with the recovery key escrowed and verified before handover (DEV-03 §5). Not after handover. This is the step whose omission produces escrow gaps.
steps.label: Built to the DEV-02 baseline, encrypted…

steps.text: Handed over with the standard software set (DEV-11), the person signed in, OneDrive known-folder redirection working (M365-12), and five minutes spent showing them where their files are. The five minutes prevents a ticket.
steps.label: Handed over with the standard software…

steps.text: The device being replaced is collected at handover, not left on the desk (§9). A device that stays on the desk is a device that is still there in a year, unpatched and signed in.
steps.label: The device being replaced is collected…

steps.text: The requester states the requirement, not the product. “I need to run Adobe Premiere on 4K footage” is a requirement. “I need a MacBook Pro” is a product, and it might not even be the right one.
steps.label: The requester states the requirement, not…

steps.text: Tier 2 states in writing what the catalogue cannot do about that requirement, and what the support consequence of the exception is — a non-standard image, a driver set nobody else runs, a warranty path that differs, or a device that will be slower to fix when it breaks.
steps.label: Tier 2 states in writing what…

steps.text: Tier 4 approves or declines, in writing, with a reason either way. A declined exception gets a real explanation and an alternative; a declined exception with no explanation becomes a departmental purchase order the following month.
steps.label: Tier 4 approves or declines…

steps.text: The approval is recorded in the exception register: person, device, requirement, approver, date, and the support consequence accepted.
steps.label: The approval is recorded…

steps.text: The device is still enrolled, still meets the DEV-02 baseline, and is still refreshed on the §7 cycle. An exception is an exception to the model, never to management, encryption or compliance.
steps.label: The device is still enrolled, still…

steps.text: Exceptions are counted annually and reported with the §8 list. A rising count is evidence that the catalogue is wrong — three requests for the same thing means it belongs in §3, not in the register.
steps.label: Exceptions are counted annually and reported…

flows.head: 8. The annual refresh list, and how it becomes a budget

callouts.title: This section depends on an inventory the organization does not fully have yet
lines: Every number in the annual list comes from the device inventory. Today, with the ticketing system and Intune both holding partial truth and the estate being enrolled wave by wave, a device can be in one system and not the other — and a device in neither is invisible to this document entirely.

So the first refresh list will be an estimate, and it should be labelled as one. The reconciliation in DEV-01 §10 and DEV-02 §8 is what turns it into a forecast, and it is a precondition for asking Finance to trust the number.
Stating this openly is better than presenting a confident figure built on an incomplete inventory. The second is how a department loses credibility with a CFO once and does not get it back.

steps.text: Tier 3 extracts from inventory every device with its class, age, assigned person, cost centre and condition (DEV-01 §10).
steps.label: Tier 3 extracts from inventory every…

steps.text: Tier 2 marks the cohort due under §7, plus any device outside cohort that should be replaced early on condition, with a one-line reason.
steps.label: Tier 2 marks the cohort due…

steps.text: The list is costed at current catalogue prices, by department and cost centre, with the off-catalogue exception count from §6 shown separately.
steps.label: The list is costed at current…

steps.text: Tier 4 reviews and issues it to the CFO, ahead of the organization’s budget cycle. [ Confirm the fiscal-year dates and the date the ask must land — IT should be producing this list against Finance’s calendar, not its own. ]
steps.label: Tier 4 reviews and issues…

steps.text: Departments see their own lines and can challenge them before the budget is set, which is the point at which a challenge is useful.
steps.label: Departments see their own lines…

steps.text: Once funded, the list becomes the year’s deployment plan, scheduled by Tier 2 against the organization’s calendar — not during the first three weeks of a busy season, and not during the busy-season readiness period in DEV-06 §9.
steps.label: The list becomes the year’s deployment…

steps.text: At year end, actuals against list. A refresh plan with no look-back gets less credible every year it is presented.
steps.label: At year end, actuals against list

appendices.head: Appendix B — “What will I get?”, for publication
rows: The standard machine
A 14-inch Windows laptop with 16 GB of memory and a fast SSD, a monitor, a dock, a keyboard and a mouse. It is a good machine, and it is what most people at the organization use.
If you present
You can have the higher-spec version, which has a better screen and a bigger battery. Ask for it — it does not need a business case.
If you travel a lot
There is a lighter 13-inch option. It is genuinely lighter and the screen is genuinely smaller, so it is worth thinking about which matters more to you.
If you never leave your desk
A desktop is often the better tool and it lasts a year longer. Worth considering rather than taking a laptop by default.
If you work in design or media
There is a workstation class, and there is a Mac. Tell us what you need to run and we will work out which.
How to ask

One ticket to the service desk address. Say who it is for, what they do, and get your budget holder to approve the cost in writing on the ticket. We will tell you within two working days whether the class you asked for is the right fit.
How long it takes

Two to three weeks for a standard machine, three to five for a Mac, six to ten for a workstation. There is no same-week option — we do not hold ready-built machines. If somebody needs a computer on Monday, ask for a loaner and we will sort that out today.
If you want something that is not on the list

You can ask, and the answer is sometimes yes. Tell us what you need to be able to do rather than which machine you want, because there is often a better answer than the one you had in mind. We will give you a written yes or no with a reason.
When it gets replaced
Laptops after four years, desktops after five. We will contact you — you do not need to wait for it to break, and please do not.
What happens to your old one

We take it when we hand you the new one, wipe it properly, and either reassign it or dispose of it securely. Your files live in OneDrive and SharePoint, so nothing of yours goes with it — and if you think something might, tell us on the day and we will check together.

callouts.title: The deadline is the whole mechanism
lines: Recommended: training software requests close six weeks before the first day of the busy season. Count back six weeks from your own busy-season start. Confirm the exact dates against the organization’s calendar with the relevant department.

A request arriving in the week before a busy season will not be in the lab in the week before a busy season, and saying so in advance is kinder than discovering it together on the first day of the busy season. Packaging, licensing and testing an unfamiliar application takes days of Tier 2 time that is already committed to the readiness runbook in §9.
A deadline with no consequence is a suggestion. So: requests after the deadline are accepted, queued behind readiness work, and given an honest date — which will often be three weeks in.

steps.sub: 4.1 Requesting training software — and the deadline

steps.sub: 4.1 Requesting training software — and the deadline

steps.sub: 4.1 Requesting training software — and the deadline

steps.sub: 4.1 Requesting training software — and the deadline

title: Mobile Device Access to Organization Data
subtitle: Your phone became part of the organization’s security perimeter the day you set up Authenticator. What that means, what we can and cannot see, and what to do when you change phones.
tierText: Tier 1 — the front door handles almost everything in this document: setting up mail on a phone, the phone-change case in §9, and answering “what can you see?”. Tier 3 owns the app protection and Conditional Access configuration; Tier 4 approves full enrollment and the §10 cutover.

review: Annually, and on any change to the MFA method position in ACC-03.

flows.head: 6. Selective wipe, full wipe, and the lost phone

steps.text: The person reports it — one number, immediately, without waiting to be sure it is not just in the car (DEV-16 §2). Nobody is ever criticised for reporting a phone that turns up.
steps.label: The person reports it — one…

steps.text: Selective wipe queued for organization data. It executes when the device next has a network connection, which may be never — so this is a mitigation, not a guarantee, and it should be described that way.
steps.label: Selective wipe queued for organization data

steps.text: Sign-in sessions revoked, so a signed-in app on that phone stops working rather than continuing until its token expires.
steps.label: Sign-in sessions revoked…

steps.text: If that phone carried an MFA method — which it almost certainly did — that method is removed, and the person needs another way to sign in. This is the step that makes a lost phone urgent rather than merely annoying.
steps.label: That phone carried an MFA method —?

gate.cond: that phone carried an MFA method — which it almost certainly did — that method is removed
gate.then: and the person needs another way to sign in

steps.text: The person is verified in person or by the ACC-06 standard before any method is re-registered. A lost phone is the ideal pretext for an attacker, and the request will arrive by exactly the route real impersonation attempts arrive by.
steps.label: The person is verified in person…

steps.text: Where the phone held CONFIDENTIAL or RESTRICTED material beyond what a mailbox ordinarily holds, GOV-03 is engaged. Where it is a theft, DEV-16 §7.
steps.label: The phone held CONFIDENTIAL or RESTRICTED material?

gate.cond: the phone held CONFIDENTIAL or RESTRICTED material beyond what a mailbox ordinarily holds
gate.then: GOV-03 is engaged

callouts.title: The request IT will not action, however genuine it looks
lines: A common failure: an Authenticator request arrives at the service desk from a personal email address, on behalf of a person with a different name, and is acted on with no verification recorded.

So, explicitly: IT does not add, remove or reset an MFA method on the strength of an email from an address that is not the account holder’s organization address; on the strength of a request made by somebody else on the holder’s behalf — including a manager, an assistant, a spouse or a colleague being helpful; or because the request is urgent and the person is travelling and stuck.

Every one of those is a legitimate-sounding request that an attacker would make word for word. The verification in ACC-06 is not an obstacle to the account holder; it is the only thing standing between an attacker and the account. Where a request cannot be verified, it is declined with the script in ACC-06 Appendix B — courteously, and with the route that will work.
This applies with no exception at Tier 1, and no member of staff can waive it by seniority or by pressure (ACC-06 §10).

steps.sub: 9.1 The good path — you still have the old phone
steps.text: Before you do anything else with the new phone, install Microsoft Authenticator on it.
steps.label: Install Microsoft Authenticator…

steps.sub: 9.1 The good path — you still have the old phone
steps.text: Add your organization account as a new method from the new phone. Sign in and approve the prompt on the OLD phone — this is why doing it before the trade-in matters, and it is the whole trick.
steps.label: Add your organization account…

steps.sub: 9.1 The good path — you still have the old phone
steps.text: Confirm both methods now appear on your account, then remove the old phone’s method yourself.
steps.label: Confirm both methods now appear…

steps.sub: 9.1 The good path — you still have the old phone
steps.text: Install the organization apps on the new phone: Outlook, Teams, OneDrive. Sign in. Set the PIN or biometric when prompted (§4).
steps.label: Install the organization apps…

steps.sub: 9.1 The good path — you still have the old phone
steps.text: Only now factory-reset, sell or trade in the old phone. Signing out of the organization account is not the same as removing the device; do the reset.
steps.label: Only now factory-reset, sell or trade…

steps.sub: 9.1 The good path — you still have the old phone
steps.text: Total elapsed time: about five minutes, no ticket, no verification appointment.
steps.label: Total elapsed time

steps.sub: 9.2 The recovery path — the old phone is gone, broken or wiped
steps.text: If you have a second registered method — a security key, a passkey on a laptop, or Authenticator on a tablet — use it. This is the entire reason for having one, and no further procedure is required.
steps.label: You have a second registered method —?

gate.cond: you have a second registered method — a security key
gate.then: a passkey on a laptop, or Authenticator on a tablet — use it

steps.sub: 9.2 The recovery path — the old phone is gone, broken or wiped
steps.text: If you have no other method: contact the service desk. This is a verified recovery, not a reset, and it will take longer than you want it to.
steps.label: You have no other method: contact?

gate.cond: you have no other method: contact the service desk. This is a verified recovery
gate.then: not a reset, and it will take longer than you want it to

steps.sub: 9.2 The recovery path — the old phone is gone, broken or wiped
steps.text: IT verifies your identity to the ACC-06 standard for a method change — which is the highest verification tier the organization operates, because re-registering an MFA method is functionally the same as handing somebody the account (ACC-06 §4, §5).
steps.label: IT verifies your identity…

steps.sub: 9.2 The recovery path — the old phone is gone, broken or wiped
steps.text: IT issues a Temporary Access Pass or equivalent, valid briefly and once, forcing re-registration at next sign-in (ACC-03 §5).
steps.label: IT issues a Temporary Access Pass…

steps.sub: 9.2 The recovery path — the old phone is gone, broken or wiped
steps.text: You register at least two methods this time, and IT should insist on it rather than leaving it as advice.
steps.label: You register at least two methods…

steps.text: The verification performed, and by whom, is recorded on the ticket. Not “verified”; what was checked (ACC-06 §9).

appendices.head: Appendix A — Getting your work email on your phone, and what we can and cannot see
rows: Yes, put your organization email on your phone

Most people do, and it is genuinely useful. Install Outlook, Teams and OneDrive from your app store, sign in with your work address, and that is it. If you get stuck, the service desk will do it with you in about five minutes.
Use Outlook, not the mail app that came with your phone

We know that is a small annoyance if you have used the built-in Mail app for years. The reason is simple: we can protect organization email inside Outlook, and we cannot protect anything inside the built-in app. Everything else on your phone stays exactly as it is either way.
What we can see

That your phone exists, its make, model and operating system version, that organization apps on it are protected, and when organization data last synced. Plus the sign-in activity on your organization account, which we can see for any device including an organization laptop.
What we cannot see

Your photos. Your personal messages. Your calls. Your other apps, or which apps you have. Your browsing. Your location. Your personal email — even if it is in the same Outlook app, it is separate and we cannot touch it. We have no way to look at any of that, and we do not want one.
What we can remove, and what we cannot

We can remove organization email and organization files from organization apps — if your phone is lost, or when you leave. We cannot wipe your phone. Your photos and everything else of yours are not ours to touch and we could not do it if we tried.
What you will notice day to day

Face ID or a PIN when you open Outlook after a while. You will not be able to copy text out of organization email into a personal note, or save an organization attachment into your personal cloud storage. That is the whole of it.
What not to put on your phone

Do not download client records, job applicant files or personnel records onto a phone. Read them in the app instead. Never anything with social security numbers, card details or health information — those do not belong on a personal device at all.
Your Authenticator app is the important one

That is the app that proves you are you. Keep a passcode or Face ID on your phone — that is the real protection — and please register a second way of signing in, on something that is not your phone. A security key, or Authenticator on a tablet. It takes ninety seconds and it is the difference between a five-minute fix and an appointment with photo ID.
Getting a new phone? Do this first

Before you trade in or reset the old one: install Authenticator on the NEW phone, add your organization account to it, and approve the prompt on the OLD phone. Then check both are listed, then wipe the old phone. Five minutes, no ticket. If the old phone has already gone and you have no other sign-in method, we can still get you back in — but we will have to verify who you are properly first, and that takes longer.
If your phone is lost or stolen

Tell us straight away, even if you think it might turn up in the car. We will remove organization data from it and stop it approving sign-ins. Nobody has ever been told off for reporting a phone that then turned up.
Why we will not just take your word for it

If somebody rings us claiming to be you and asks us to move your sign-in method to a new phone, and we do it, they now have your account — your mail, your files, and everything the organization connects to it. It is a common attack. So we will always check who you are before changing anything, including when you are in a hurry, and including when it is obviously really you. It is not about you; it is the only thing protecting you.
If you would rather not have organization email on your phone
Then do not. There is no expectation and no consequence. Outlook on the web works fine from any browser, and plenty of people prefer to leave work at work.

title: macOS Device Management Standard
subtitle: The target state the macOS enrollment pilot can be judged against — mapped condition by condition onto the Windows baseline, so the two platforms are comparable rather than divergent.
tierText: Tier 2 — Advanced Technical Services enrolls, builds and supports Macs. Tier 3 owns the Apple Business Manager relationship, the Intune configuration and the Platform SSO deployment. Tier 4 declares the pilot production against §12.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and every autumn when Apple ships a major macOS release — the release cadence is the single largest recurring risk in this document.

flows.head: 3. Enrollment — ABM, ADE, and the devices that cannot be ADE-enrolled

callouts.title: Be straight about this: a Mac bought retail cannot be ADE-enrolled. Ever.
lines: ADE depends on the device having entered the organization’s Apple Business Manager account at the point of purchase, through Apple or an authorised reseller who does that enrollment. A Mac bought from a consumer retailer, bought online on a personal card and expensed, or bought through a project budget from an unlinked supplier, cannot be added to ABM afterwards. There is no retrospective path, no support call that fixes it, and no workaround. The device can only ever be manually enrolled.

The consequence is a permanent, documented compliance gap on that device: management is removable by its user, supervision-dependent restrictions cannot be applied, and the account-creation control in §6 was never available — so its first user is almost certainly a local administrator.
This is not a small administrative irritation. It is the difference between a managed Mac and a Mac that is managed until somebody decides otherwise.

steps.sub: 3.1 The purchasing rule that stops it recurring
steps.text: Every Mac and every iPad the organization buys is purchased through the ABM-linked channel. This is a rule in DEV-04 §3 (class S6), not a preference, and it applies to project-funded and departmentally-funded purchases identically.
steps.label: Every Mac and every iPad…

steps.sub: 3.1 The purchasing rule that stops it recurring
steps.text: No Mac is bought on a personal card and expensed. The reimbursement route is the commonest way an unmanageable Mac enters the organization, and the person doing it is being helpful rather than difficult — which is why the rule has to be published rather than enforced by refusal at the finance desk.
steps.label: No Mac is bought…

steps.sub: 3.1 The purchasing rule that stops it recurring
steps.text: Project purchases: a project budget can specify a Mac; it cannot specify a supplier that leaves the organization with an unmanageable device. IT supplies the channel details to Procurement so this is settled when the budget is approved rather than at delivery.
steps.label: Project purchases…

steps.sub: 3.1 The purchasing rule that stops it recurring
steps.text: Where a device has already arrived outside the channel, it is manually enrolled (§11), and the gap is recorded against it in inventory with the reason. Not hidden, and not treated as compliant.
steps.label: A device has already arrived outside?

gate.cond: a device has already arrived outside the channel
gate.then: it is manually enrolled (§11), and the gap is recorded against it in inventory with the reason

steps.sub: 3.1 The purchasing rule that stops it recurring
steps.text: The count of non-ADE Macs is reported annually with the DEV-04 §8 refresh list. It should fall every year; if it does not, the purchasing rule is not operating.
steps.label: The count of non-ADE Macs…

steps.sub: 3.1 The purchasing rule that stops it recurring
steps.text: The gap closes at refresh. A non-ADE Mac is replaced at its four-year point by an ADE-enrolled one, which makes this a bounded problem with an end date rather than a permanent condition.
steps.label: The gap closes at refresh

flows.name: Enrollment — ABM, ADE, and the devices that cannot be ADE-enrolled

callouts.title: This is the BitLocker escrow problem again, on a different platform.
lines: A move between encryption tools typically only reaches machines that are online and healthy. Afterwards some devices show a BitLocker key in Entra and some show nothing, and without a procedure nobody can tell which is which (DEV-03).

FileVault has precisely the same failure mode. A Mac with FileVault on and no escrowed recovery key is not a protected device — it is a device whose data is gone the moment it needs recovering. The user cannot help; the key does not exist anywhere else.

The difference is that the failure is now known. There is no excuse for arriving at the same position on a second platform, which is why escrow verification is exit criterion 3 in §12 and appears twice in Appendix A.

steps.text: FileVault is enabled by configuration profile at enrollment, not left to the user and not enabled after handover.
steps.label: FileVault is enabled by configuration profile…

steps.text: The personal recovery key is escrowed to Intune. Escrow is configured before enablement — a key generated before escrow is configured is not retrospectively collected.
steps.label: The personal recovery key is escrowed…

steps.text: Escrow is VERIFIED per device, by querying for the key, before the Mac is handed to anybody. Verified means somebody looked and the key was there. Not “the policy is assigned”.
steps.label: Escrow is VERIFIED per device…

steps.text: Key rotation is enabled so that a key used once is replaced automatically.
steps.label: Key rotation is enabled…

steps.text: Tier 3 runs the same detection query monthly that DEV-03 §5 runs for Windows: every enrolled Mac, encryption state, and escrow present or absent. The three-number position — encrypted with key, encrypted without key, not encrypted — is reported with the DEV-03 figures rather than separately, so nobody reads a Windows number and believes it covers the estate.
steps.label: Tier 3 runs the same detection…

steps.text: Remediation for a Mac with no escrowed key: confirm escrow configuration is applied, then rotate the key so a fresh one is generated and escrowed, then verify. Where the Mac cannot be brought into escrow at all — an unmanaged machine, or a user-encrypted volume — the device is recorded as an exception with an owner and a date, and it is not treated as compliant.
steps.label: Remediation for a Mac with no…

steps.text: Retrieving a key for a user: the requester is verified to the ACC-06 standard before the key is released, and the release is recorded — who asked, who verified, who released, on which device (DEV-03 §7). A recovery key is a key to everything on the machine, and the request will sometimes arrive by the route real impersonation attempts arrive by.
steps.label: Retrieving a key for a user

steps.text: Before any wipe, reimage, reassignment or disposal: escrow state is checked and the key retained until the device is confirmed clear (DEV-03 §8, DEV-15). A Mac wiped on the assumption that a key exists is unrecoverable if it did not.
steps.label: Reimage, reassignment or disposal

flows.head: 11. Migrating the Macs that already exist

steps.text: Enumerate them. Model, age, OS version, who has it, what it is used for, whether it was bought through the ABM channel, and whether its user holds admin. Until this list exists the organization does not know the size of the problem (§2).
steps.label: Enumerate them

steps.text: Triage on hardware and OS. A Mac too old for a supported macOS is a DEV-04 §8 refresh line, not a migration task. Spending Tier 2 time enrolling a machine that will be replaced within the year is the wrong order of work.
steps.label: Triage on hardware and OS

steps.text: Talk to the users first, individually, and tell them what will change and what will not. This population is small enough to make that possible and technical enough to notice if it is not done.
steps.label: Talk to the users first, individually…

steps.text: Enroll via Company Portal. User data stays in place; this is not a rebuild.
steps.label: Enroll via Company Portal

steps.text: Apply the §4 baseline, then enable FileVault and — before anything else is considered finished — VERIFY the escrowed key exists (§5). On an already-encrypted Mac the existing key is not escrowed retrospectively: rotate it so a fresh key is generated and captured.
steps.label: Apply the baseline, then enable…

steps.text: Deploy Platform SSO and the standard application set. Record the local account short name and resolve any mismatch with the Entra UPN now, not later (§7).
steps.label: Deploy Platform SSO and the standard…

steps.text: Onboard Defender with its permission profiles, and confirm it can actually see the disk (§10.1).
steps.label: Onboard Defender with its permission profiles…

steps.text: Set update deferral before the next macOS major, whichever month the migration happens in (§9).
steps.label: Set update deferral before the next…

steps.text: Record the device in inventory, with the ADE gap flagged where it applies, and a refresh date that closes the gap (§3.1 step 6).
steps.label: Record the device in inventory…

steps.text: Only now address standing admin (§6). Last, deliberately: by this point the machine is managed, encrypted, escrowed, protected and patched, so if the admin conversation takes three months the organization is not exposed while it happens.
steps.label: Only now address standing admin

title: Software Request, Approval, Licensing & Deployment
subtitle: How a request for software is answered — the “do we already have it?” check, the approval path by cost and by risk, the licence register, and the deployment mechanism of record through a move to Intune.
tierText: Tier 2 — Advanced Technical Services runs intake, packaging and deployment. Tier 3 owns the security and compatibility assessment and the deployment mechanism. Tier 4 approves cost and anything material. Tier 1 answers “where do I get X?” from the published catalogue rather than raising a request.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend Head of IT, with the CFO on §4 ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and at each renewal cycle.

steps.text: WHAT: the exact product, edition and version. “Adobe” is not a product; “Acrobat Pro, current subscription release” is.
steps.label: WHAT

steps.text: WHY: what it is for, in one sentence a non-specialist can read. This is the field the approvers actually read.
steps.label: WHY

steps.text: WHO: how many people, named or by role, and whether the number is expected to grow.
steps.label: WHO

steps.text: DATA: does it hold, process or transmit client records, payroll or HR data, or anything in the sensitive classes in M365-15? A yes routes to §5 whatever the cost.
steps.label: DATA…

steps.text: WHERE: does the data stay on the device, sit in the organization tenant, or go to a vendor’s cloud? If the last, in which country, and does the vendor use organization data to train anything?
steps.label: The last?

gate.cond: the last
gate.then: in which country, and does the vendor use organization data to train anything?

steps.text: COST: one-off and recurring, per seat or per device, and the funding source with the budget holder named.
steps.label: COST

steps.text: WHEN: the date it is needed, and what depends on it. “As soon as possible” sets no priority (GOV-06 §4).
steps.label: WHEN?

steps.text: RIGHTS: does it need administrative rights to install, or to run? Those are two different answers and the second is the expensive one (§10, DEV-12).
steps.label: RIGHTS

steps.text: SIGN-IN: does it authenticate against organization identity? If so it is also an ACC-16 intake and the two run together, not one after the other.
steps.label: SIGN-IN

steps.text: PLACE: individual devices, a departmental set, or a lab or meeting-room image? A lab image change lands in a quiet-period window (DEV-06, GOV-04 §7).
steps.label: PLACE

steps.text: ALREADY THERE: has a trial already been installed, and on how many machines? Asked without reproach, because the honest answer is frequently yes and IT needs to know what is on the estate more than it needs to be right about how it got there.
steps.label: ALREADY THERE

steps.text: ALTERNATIVE: what was checked at §2, and why it does not fit.
steps.label: ALTERNATIVE

callouts.title: An extension is software with the fewest controls and the widest reach.
lines: Installing one takes a click. It needs no administrative rights, generates no ticket, appears in no inventory today, and asks its permission question at the moment the person is trying to get something done — so the answer is always yes.

What it can then do is read and modify every page the person visits. That includes the HR system, the payroll screens, the mailbox, the client records system and anything else that lives in a browser, which in most organizations is now most things. An extension is closer to a credential than to an application.
Extensions also change hands. A benign extension with a large install base is a saleable asset, and the new owner inherits the permissions the original earned. The user is not asked again.

steps.text: MEASURE. Report what extensions are installed across the estate. This is the number that will surprise people and it does not exist today.
steps.label: MEASURE

steps.text: Publish the allow list, derived from what is actually in use and defensible — a password manager, an accessibility tool, a citation manager, a screen-reader helper, whatever the measurement shows people genuinely rely on.
steps.label: Publish the allow list, derived…

steps.text: Tell people, name a date, and give them the route in §3 for anything missing. A fortnight’s notice removes most of the friction.
steps.label: Tell people, name a date…

steps.text: Then enforce, blocking by default. Not before — enforcing against a population that cannot comply is the DEV-02 §2 failure and the organization has already paid for that lesson once.
steps.label: Then enforce, blocking by default

steps.text: The ACC-01 leaver checklist includes non-Microsoft named-user licences held by the leaver, taken from the register (§6) rather than from anybody’s memory.
steps.label: The ACC-01 leaver checklist includes non-Microsoft…

steps.text: Each is either reassigned — where the terms permit it (§6) — or released, and the register updated with the date. Not “to be tidied up later”.
steps.label: Each is either reassigned — where…

steps.text: Wiping and re-provisioning the device removes the installation (DEV-15 §4). It does not release the vendor-side seat. Those are two separate actions and both are needed; doing only the first is how entitled and deployed counts drift apart.
steps.label: Wiping and re-provisioning the device removes…

steps.text: Where the leaver was the BUSINESS OWNER of a product in the register, that is a trigger in its own right: the product needs a new owner before the next renewal, or it is a candidate for retirement (the same pattern as a departing sponsor in ACC-10 §3).

appendices.head: Appendix A — The software request form
rows: Requester and department
Named person. A department is not a requester.
Product, edition, version
Exact. “Adobe” is not a product.
What it is for
One sentence, readable by a non-specialist. This is the field the approvers read.
Who will use it
How many, named or by role, and whether the number will grow.
Does it touch client, payroll or HR data?
Yes / No / Not sure. “Not sure” routes to §5 and is a perfectly good answer.
Where does the data go?
On the device, in the organization tenant, or to a vendor. If a vendor: which country, and do they use organization data to train anything?
Cost
One-off and recurring, per seat or per device, with the funding source and the budget holder named.
When is it needed, and what depends on it
A date and a reason. “As soon as possible” sets no priority.
Administrative rights
Needed to install? Needed to run? Two separate answers.
Does it sign in with an organization account?
If yes, this is also an ACC-16 intake and they run together.
Where does it go?
Individual devices, a departmental set, or a lab or meeting-room image.
Already installed anywhere?
Including trials. Asked without reproach — IT needs to know what is on the estate.
What was checked at §2, and why it does not fit
The one question that closes the most requests, honestly, in ten minutes.

appendices.head: Appendix B — The security review questions IT asks
rows: Where does the software come from, and how will it be obtained?
Provenance is the largest single risk in free software (§7). The vendor’s own site or a recognised repository, verified where a signature or checksum exists.
What does it reach — the device only, the network, or the internet?
Determines whether this is a desktop decision or a network and data decision.
Does it hold, process or transmit client records, payroll or HR data?
Routes the request to Tier 4 whatever it costs, including free. The sensitive classes in M365-15 apply.
Where does the data physically live, and who else can see it?
A vendor cloud is a data transfer. Sub-processors and training use are both fair questions and are frequently answered in the terms.
How does a person sign in?
organization identity via ACC-16, or its own password store — which means another credential, no MFA, and no leaver process.
How is a leaver removed?
SCIM, an admin console, or nothing. Nothing means the ACC-17 §2 annual review is the only control that will ever reach it (ACC-16 §7).
Does it request tenant consent or OAuth permissions?
That is an application identity with standing permissions, not an install. ACC-08 §8.
Does it need administrative rights to install, or to run?
To run is a DEV-12 exception and a standing weakening of the endpoint (§10).
Who patches it, and how does an update reach the estate?
Vendor channel, a managed package, or an unmanaged auto-updater. DEV-13 §3 has to be able to answer this before deployment, not after.
Does it install a driver, a service, or its own real-time protection?
A second protection product on one device is a fault (DEV-14 §4). A kernel driver is a stability and support question as well as a security one.
Does it need an inbound firewall rule, an open port, or a vendor VPN?
A network change under GOV-04 and a remote-access decision under DEV-10, both of which can cost more than the software.
What happens if the organization stops using it?
Can the data be extracted, in what format, and by whom? Asked at the start, because it cannot be asked usefully at the end.

title: Patch, Update & Maintenance Window Standard
subtitle: Eight classes of estate in one governing table, remediation timeframes the department can actually hold — and the rule that a vendor patch is an organization change.
tierText: Tier 3 — Expert Services owns the update rings, the server and infrastructure regime, and the vulnerability triage. Tier 2 executes endpoint, lab and meeting room patching. Tier 4 approves exceptions and emergency changes and receives the monthly position.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Every six months while the Intune transition is live, then annually.

steps.text: Read the advisories on publication day and identify anything critical or actively exploited, which leaves this cycle and goes to §10.
steps.label: Read the advisories on publication day…

steps.text: Raise the change record under GOV-04 §4, with the back-out, before any work begins. Standing monthly patching is approved once as a standard change; each cycle is then a register entry rather than a fresh approval (GOV-04 §3).
steps.label: Raise the change record under GOV-04…

steps.text: Confirm a backup or snapshot exists and is verified. “There is a backup” and “the backup restores” are different statements, and the difference is discovered at the worst moment.
steps.label: Confirm a backup or snapshot exists…

steps.text: Apply to TEST, and leave it for a stated interval — seven days for a routine month. Shorter only under §10, and the shortened interval is recorded as a decision rather than as an omission.
steps.label: Apply to TEST, and leave…

steps.text: Apply to PRODUCTION in the window, in a stated order, with the most consequential system last where sequencing permits.
steps.label: Apply to PRODUCTION in the window…

steps.text: Verify against a stated check: services running, an application transaction completed, a report produced. “It booted” is not a verification and neither is “the vendor said it went fine” (GOV-04 §8).
steps.label: Verify against a stated check

steps.text: Record the ACTUAL start and finish times on the change record. Correlating a change with the tickets it produced is the main day-to-day use of the register and an approximate date defeats it (GOV-04 §4).
steps.label: Record the ACTUAL start and finish…

flows.head: 7. Vendor-managed systems — the evidence base, and the rule

callouts.title: A vendor patch is an organization change. The rule is GOV-04 §8; what follows is its patching shape.
lines: It enters the GOV-04 register, with a named organization approver, a back-out, a test-before-production sequence and a communication — whoever executes it, however routine, and however competent the vendor.

Nothing in the remediation described in §1 is done badly. Test precedes Production, the work sits inside the window, and the engineer is careful. The gap is entirely the record: the organization cannot reconstruct what was applied, could not have told the vendor “not that week” if that week had been a peak week, and has nothing to point at three months later when something on that system behaves oddly.
The vendor’s own change process is their internal control. It is not the organization’s record, and it is not visible to anybody at the organization.

steps.text: Approve standing vendor maintenance ONCE, as a standing change with a defined scope, a named window and a stated back-out (GOV-04 §8 step 6). Each execution is then a one-line register entry. This is what stops the process being abandoned for the routine work it was never meant to obstruct.
steps.label: Approve standing vendor maintenance ONCE…

steps.text: Name an organization approver. The vendor is never the approver of a change to an organization system — not because their judgement is doubted, but because approval is an accountability the organization cannot outsource.
steps.label: Name an organization approver

steps.text: Give the vendor the freeze calendar a quarter in advance (GOV-04 §7.1). Peak business weeks are not negotiable, and the usual reason an organization cannot say so is that nobody told the vendor what the freezes were.
steps.label: Give the vendor the freeze calendar…

steps.text: Have an organization engineer reachable during the window — not necessarily executing, but able to verify afterwards and to escalate if the window overruns.
steps.label: The window overruns?

steps.text: Verify against the organization’s own check and record it (§6.1 step 6).
steps.label: Verify against the organization’s own check…

steps.text: Confirm the access the vendor used was a named vendor account, time-boxed rather than standing, and logged (ACC-11 §6, ACC-11 §7). A patch applied through a shared credential is unattributable afterwards.
steps.label: Confirm the access the vendor used…

steps.text: Put the requirement into the contract at renewal (ACC-11 §10). Until it is there, this section depends on goodwill — which is worth having, and is not a control.
steps.label: Put the requirement into the contract…

appendices.head: Appendix B — The vulnerability triage decision table
rows: Is it actively exploited, on the CISA KEV list, or exploited in our own estate?
Treat as CRITICAL whatever the CVSS score. Out-of-band under §10, today. Tier 3 now, and Tier 4 informed.
Is the affected asset internet-facing or externally reachable?
48 hours for critical, and it does not extend in any capacity state (§8). High takes the tighter figure.
Does the asset hold the sensitive classes in M365-15?
Take the tighter figure. Where exposure is credible rather than theoretical, GOV-03 before patching — preserve before you fix (GOV-03 §6).
Is the fix something the organization controls?
Yes: assign a named owner and a target date from §8. No: §7 — raise it with the vendor, record the date raised and the date they give, and track it as open.
Is there a patch at all?
No patch: mitigate — a configuration change, a disabled feature, isolation — and re-date. A mitigation is not a closure and it carries an expiry (§9.3).
Is the affected software still needed?
Removing it closes the item permanently and is frequently faster than patching it. Ask before assuming (DEV-11 §11).
Will the patch break something known?
A §11 exception: compensating control, expiry, Tier 4 approver. Ring 3 (§4) is where the device goes. Not a silent deferral.
Is the system past vendor support?
Not an exception — there is nothing to defer. A Tier 4 accepted risk with an end date and a replacement plan (§11).
Does it affect a vendor-managed system?
§7. It enters the GOV-04 register as a vendor change with an organization approver, whoever applies it.
Has it actually been remediated?
Verify in the platform, not from memory. Close with the evidence and the date.
None of the above?
It stays open. Ageing out of the console view is not closure (§9.3).
