title: Endpoint Security Agent & MDR Escalation Standard
subtitle: How many devices actually have a healthy agent reporting — and then who acts on an MDR case, in what time, on whose authority, and what closes it.
tierText: Tier 3 — Expert Services owns the agent estate and the MDR relationship. Tier 2 remediates unhealthy agents and executes containment within §6. Tier 4 authorises isolation above the §6 threshold and declares incidents under GOV-03.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Every six months, and after any change to the MDR service description.

flows.head: 3. Measuring coverage, and the path for a device that has stopped reporting

steps.text: PRODUCE THE NUMBER. Devices in the authoritative asset record (DEV-01 §10) as the denominator, against devices with an agent that has reported within the last 7 days as the numerator. State both figures and the ratio, with a date. Do not start from the security console: it can only show what reported, which makes the denominator wrong and the resulting number flattering.
steps.label: PRODUCE THE NUMBER

steps.text: RECONCILE THE TWO INVENTORIES, both directions. A device in the asset record and not in the console is the gap this document exists for. A device in the console and not in the asset record is also a finding — it is unmanaged, or it is somebody’s personal machine, or it is a decommissioned device never removed (DEV-15).
steps.label: RECONCILE THE TWO INVENTORIES, both directions

steps.text: CLASSIFY THE GAP, because the remediation differs entirely: never enrolled (DEV-01); enrolled but the agent never installed; agent installed and unhealthy; agent healthy but not reporting, which is usually network, proxy or an exclusion; and genuinely retired but never removed from the record.
steps.label: CLASSIFY THE GAP, because the remediation…

steps.text: SET AND PUBLISH THE TARGET: 98% of the managed Windows estate reporting within 7 days, measured monthly. Not 100% — devices are legitimately switched off for weeks, in a drawer, or in transit, and a 100% target makes the figure a fiction nobody investigates. 98% with a named list of the remainder is a number somebody can act on.
steps.label: SET AND PUBLISH THE TARGET

steps.text: CHASE THE REMAINDER INDIVIDUALLY. This is the step that will not happen by itself, and it is the step that matters most. A silent device does not remediate itself and it does not appear as a failure — it simply does not appear.
steps.label: CHASE THE REMAINDER INDIVIDUALLY

steps.text: GIVE THE NUMBER A STANDING HOME: the monthly position in §12, and the DEV-02 §10 three-number report. A coverage figure produced once for a meeting decays immediately.
steps.label: GIVE THE NUMBER A STANDING HOME

steps.text: ONLY THEN treat MDR case volume as meaningful. A quiet month on partial coverage is not a quiet month, and reporting it as one is worse than not reporting at all.
steps.label: ONLY THEN treat MDR case volume…

flows.name: Measuring coverage, and the path for a device that has stopped reporting

steps.text: THE ORGANIZATION HAS RECORDED AN OUTCOME: remediated; contained with no further action; no incident, with the reason; or escalated to GOV-03.
steps.label: THE ORGANIZATION HAS RECORDED AN OUTCOME

steps.text: CONTAINMENT HELD. No further activity from the identity, device or infrastructure involved, across a stated observation period — 48 hours for a confirmed compromise.
steps.label: CONTAINMENT HELD

steps.text: SCOPE WAS ASSESSED, NOT ASSUMED. What else did this identity or device touch? One compromised account is rarely the whole picture (GOV-03 §5 step 6).
steps.label: SCOPE WAS ASSESSED, NOT ASSUMED

steps.text: ANY ISOLATION OR ACCOUNT DISABLEMENT HAS BEEN LIFTED, or its continuation is recorded with a reason and a review date (§6).
steps.label: ANY ISOLATION OR ACCOUNT DISABLEMENT HAS…

steps.text: THE AFFECTED PERSON HAS BEEN TOLD, through a channel independent of the affected account (GOV-03 §7). Including where the answer turned out to be nothing — especially then.
steps.label: THE AFFECTED PERSON HAS BEEN TOLD…

steps.text: THE AGENT ON THE AFFECTED DEVICE IS HEALTHY AND REPORTING (§3.2). A remediated device that is now silent is not remediated; it is invisible.
steps.label: THE AGENT ON THE AFFECTED DEVICE…

steps.text: THE PARTNER’S RECORD MATCHES THE ORGANIZATION’S. Closed on their side with the organization’s outcome — not left open, and not closed with a guess (GOV-03 §8).
steps.label: THE PARTNER’S RECORD MATCHES THE ORGANIZATION’S

steps.text: WHERE THE CAUSE WAS A CONTROL GAP, it is raised against the relevant SOP under GOV-01 §7 rather than remembered. Several documents in this catalogue exist by exactly that route.
steps.label: THE CAUSE WAS A CONTROL GAP?

gate.cond: THE CAUSE WAS A CONTROL GAP
gate.then: it is raised against the relevant SOP under GOV-01 §7 rather than remembered

title: Printer, Copier & Peripheral Standard
subtitle: The most frequent request the front door receives and the least severe. Written down once so it stops being answered forty times — and because a copier is a computer with a hard drive in it.
tierText: Tier 1 — the published model names peripherals, printers and hardware as front-door work, and this document is written so that the front door can finish the job. Tier 2 owns queue and driver deployment; Tier 3 owns the print architecture decision in §4; Tier 4 owns the exceptions in §2 and the disposal approvals in §11.

flows.head: 3. Adding a printer on a managed device

callouts.title: So the first diagnostic question is not “how do I add it”
lines: If a managed device does not already have the printers for its area, that is a deployment gap and it belongs in a ticket against the assignment, not in a walk-through with the user. Adding it by hand fixes one person and leaves the next twelve to discover the same thing.

Tier 1 adds the printer by hand to unblock the person in front of them, and then records that the assignment did not reach the device. Both halves. The second half is the one that stops the ticket recurring.

steps.text: Confirm the device is enrolled and compliant. An unenrolled device is a DEV-01 matter and printing is a symptom, not the problem.
steps.label: Confirm the device is enrolled…

steps.text: Confirm which printer they should have — by room or department, from the printer register. Guessing produces a queue that works today and points at the wrong floor after the next move.
steps.label: Confirm which printer they should have…

steps.text: Add it per Appendix B, which is written to be handed to the user.
steps.label: Add it per Appendix B, which…

steps.text: Print a test page before leaving or ending the contact. A printer that was added but never printed is not a closed ticket.
steps.label: Print a test page before leaving…

steps.text: Where secure release applies, have the person release the test job at the device with their badge or PIN, so that the first time they use it is not the day it matters (§5).
steps.label: Secure release applies?

gate.cond: secure release applies
gate.then: have the person release the test job at the device with their badge or PIN, so that the first time they use it is not the day it matters (§5)

steps.text: Record the deployment gap if there was one. Assignment groups are corrected in batches, and the batch is built from these records.
steps.label: There was one?

gate.cond: there was one. Assignment groups are corrected in batches
gate.then: and the batch is built from these records

flows.name: Adding a printer on a managed device

flows.head: 6. Scanning — to email, to OneDrive, and the relay trap

callouts.title: A copier configured to send through an unauthenticated relay is a mail security hole with a paper feeder
lines: The convenient way to make scan-to-email work is to point the device at something that will accept mail from it without credentials. Every copier vendor knows how to do this and it takes four minutes.

What the organization then has is a device on the network that will send mail appearing to come from the organization, to anybody, at the request of anybody who can walk up to it. It bypasses the external-mail banner, the phishing controls and any content inspection (M365-22). It is also, eventually, found — open relays are scanned for continuously, and the organization learns about it from a blocklist rather than from an audit.

The rule: a multifunction device sends mail by authenticated submission, using a dedicated non-human account under ACC-08 with a named owner and a rotation schedule — never a person’s credentials, and never a shared password recorded in the device’s configuration page and nowhere else.

And it sends to internal recipients only, unless a specific business need is approved by Tier 4 with a recorded reason. Scan-to-external from a walk-up device is an unmonitored data export channel with no sender identity behind it.

steps.sub: 6.2 Scan to email, and the trap
steps.text: The sending account is created and owned under ACC-08. Its credential is held in custody, not in the technician’s notes.
steps.label: The sending account is created…

steps.sub: 6.2 Scan to email, and the trap
steps.text: The from-address is a device address that is obviously a device — a scanner address, not a person and not a department that receives mail. Replies to a scan should bounce somewhere harmless.
steps.label: The from-address is a device address…

steps.sub: 6.2 Scan to email, and the trap
steps.text: Recipients are restricted to internal addresses at the transport level, so the restriction survives somebody changing the device’s address book.
steps.label: Recipients are restricted to internal addresses…

steps.sub: 6.2 Scan to email, and the trap
steps.text: The device’s own address book is treated as a directory extract and is reviewed when the device is reconfigured or relocated. Leavers accumulate in it (ACC-01 §7.2).
steps.label: The device’s own address book…

steps.sub: 6.2 Scan to email, and the trap
steps.text: Scan-to-self — the device mails the scan to the signed-in user and nobody else — is the safest form of scan-to-email and should be preferred where the platform supports it.
steps.label: Scan-to-self — the device mails…

steps.sub: 6.2 Scan to email, and the trap
steps.text: Never scan anything in the sensitive classes to a personal address. Say it in the end-user guidance, because it is the single most common informal workaround in any institution.
steps.label: Never scan anything in the sensitive…

flows.name: Scanning — to email, to OneDrive, and the relay trap

flows.head: 8. The copier fleet and vendor service calls

callouts.title: Say this plainly, because it is invisible in the way a remote access grant is not
lines: A copier engineer arrives, unaccompanied, with tools and a bag, and works for an hour on a networked device that holds images of everything the department has scanned. Nobody logged in. No account was created. No ticket in the identity register records that an outside party had hands-on access to an organization system.

The controls in ACC-11 — named individuals, notification of changes, purpose limitation, screening appropriate to the access held, and the right to audit — are written for accounts. They apply with at least equal force to a person physically in the building, and many organizations have no document that says so.

ACTION: the physical escort and sign-in expectation for vendor technicians should be recorded either in ACC-11 §8 or in a Facilities procedure, and cross-referenced from here. Raised as a gap rather than legislated here, because it is not IT’s to own alone. Owner: a named IT lead, with Facilities and site security.

steps.text: The fault is reported to the service desk, which logs it with the vendor. Departments calling the vendor directly produces a fleet whose fault history exists only in the vendor’s system, which is where the register in DEV-18 §11 and the refresh case in DEV-04 both come from.
steps.label: The fault is reported…

steps.text: The ticket records the device asset tag, location, error code and the vendor reference. The vendor reference is the field people forget and the one that makes the follow-up possible.
steps.label: The ticket records the device asset…

steps.text: The requesting department is told when the technician is expected, so that somebody is there and the room is accessible.
steps.label: The requesting department is told…

steps.sub: 8.2 A vendor technician on site is a physical access event
steps.text: The technician signs in at the point the organization normally requires, and is met by a member of the department or of IT. “Met” is not “escorted at all times” for a copier in a corridor; it is “somebody knows they are here and who they are”.
steps.label: The technician signs…

steps.sub: 8.2 A vendor technician on site is a physical access event
steps.text: Where the device sits in a restricted area — a payroll office, a records room, a server room — the technician is accompanied for the duration. Not as a comment on the technician.
steps.label: The device sits in a restricted area?

gate.cond: the device sits in a restricted area — a payroll office
gate.then: a records room, a server room — the technician is accompanied for the duration

steps.sub: 8.2 A vendor technician on site is a physical access event
steps.text: Nothing leaves the building without the organization knowing what it is. A replaced part is a part; a replaced hard drive or storage board is a data event and §11 applies to it before it goes anywhere.
steps.label: Nothing leaves the building without…

steps.sub: 8.2 A vendor technician on site is a physical access event
steps.text: Remote fleet management access held by the vendor — the tool that reads meters and pushes firmware — is a vendor access grant under ACC-11 with a named owner, and it is in scope for the quarterly vendor access review, not exempt because it is “just the copiers”.
steps.label: Remote fleet management access held…

steps.sub: 8.2 A vendor technician on site is a physical access event
steps.text: Firmware updates pushed by the vendor are changes to a networked device on the organization estate. They belong in the change record (GOV-04) even when the vendor treats them as routine, and they do not happen during a period when the device is needed.
steps.label: Firmware updates pushed by the vendor…

flows.name: The copier fleet and vendor service calls

flows.head: 11. Disposal — a copier is a computer

callouts.title: The multifunction device in the corridor has a hard drive in it, and the drive holds images of what it has processed
lines: Print jobs, scans, copies, faxes, held secure-release jobs, the address book, and in many models a spooled image of every document that has passed through it. Depending on configuration and model, that can be months of a department’s paperwork.

It leaves the building at end of lease, on a date set by a contract, collected by a logistics firm, and it goes to a vendor’s refurbishment floor. Unless somebody acts, the drive goes with it. This is the single highest-consequence sentence in this document and it belongs to a P3 because nobody has ever raised a ticket about it.

DEV-15 governs the handling. The organization’s existing Disposal of Sensitive Data Policy governs the obligation. Both apply to a copier exactly as they apply to a laptop, and the fact that it does not look like a computer is not a distinction the policy makes.

steps.text: Every multifunction device on the estate is in the asset register with a note of whether it holds a drive and whether that drive is encrypted. Most modern fleet devices support both encryption and an overwrite-on-completion setting; both should be on, and it is worth finding out whether they are.
steps.label: Every multifunction device on the estate…

steps.text: End-of-lease dates are held by IT and by whoever holds the contract, and they are diarised. A device leaving on a contractual date with no action taken is the failure mode, and it happens because the date lives in a finance system rather than in an IT calendar.
steps.label: End-of-lease dates are held…

steps.text: Before any device leaves — end of lease, replacement, or vendor exchange — the drive is sanitised to the DEV-15 standard, or removed and destroyed and the device leaves without it. Which of those is available depends on the lease terms, so it is a question to ask at contract signature, not at collection.
steps.label: Replacement, or vendor exchange —…

steps.text: Obtain the certificate. A vendor assurance that “the drives are wiped” is not a record; a certificate naming the device, the serial, the method and the date is. It is retained per DEV-15.
steps.label: Obtain the certificate

steps.text: Clear the address book, the stored credentials, the scan destinations and the sending account before release, and rotate the ACC-08 sending credential that device used (§6). A retired copier’s configuration page has held a working credential more than once, somewhere.
steps.label: Clear the address book, the stored…

steps.text: The same applies to a device being relocated between departments, which is the case everybody forgets. A copier moving from Finance to a shared corridor carries Finance’s held jobs and Finance’s address book with it. Treat a relocation as a reassignment under DEV-15.
steps.label: The same applies to a device…

steps.text: Small peripherals with no storage — cables, keyboards, mice, monitors — are not a data risk and go to standard e-waste. Anything with storage in it, including some newer desk phones and conferencing devices, is not in that category.
steps.label: Small peripherals with no storage —…

flows.name: Disposal — a copier is a computer

flows.head: Appendix A — “It will not print”: the Tier 1 troubleshooting ladder

steps.text: Look at the printer itself. Nine times out of ten it is telling you what is wrong on its little screen — out of paper, a door open, a tray not pushed in, toner low, a paper jam. Fix what it says and try again. This is the first step because it is the answer more often than everything below it put together.
steps.label: Look at the printer itself

steps.text: Check you are printing to the printer you are standing next to. It sounds obvious. It is the most common cause of a job that vanished — it printed perfectly, on another floor. Look at the printer name in the print window before you press print, and check the name on the sticker on the machine.
steps.label: Check you are printing…

steps.text: If this is a secure-release printer, your job is waiting for you. Nothing comes out until you tap your card or enter your PIN at the machine. If you have never done this before, come to the service desk and we will set you up in two minutes.
steps.label: This is a secure-release printer?

gate.cond: this is a secure-release printer
gate.then: your job is waiting for you

steps.text: Open your print queue and see whether the job is sitting there. On Windows, click the printer icon near the clock, or open Settings and find your printer. If there is a stuck job at the top of the list, delete everything in the queue and print once — just once. Printing four more times while one is stuck is how six copies appear an hour later.
steps.label: Open your print queue and see…

steps.text: Turn the printer off, wait ten seconds, turn it back on. Give it a minute to come back. This resolves a genuine share of faults and costs you two minutes.
steps.label: Turn the printer off, wait ten…

steps.text: Restart your computer. We know. It genuinely fixes the print service when it has got itself into a state, and it is faster than waiting for us.
steps.label: Restart your computer

steps.text: Find out whether it is just you. Ask the person next to you to print something. If nobody can print, it is the printer and we already want to know. If it is only you, it is your computer or your queue and the steps below are the ones that will help.
steps.label: Find out whether it is just…

steps.text: Try printing something else — one page from a different document, or a test page from the printer settings. If that works, the problem is the document you were trying to print, not the printer. Very large files, files with unusual fonts, and PDFs from outside the organization are the usual suspects. Save it as a PDF and print that.
steps.label: Try printing something else — one…

steps.text: Remove the printer and add it back. Appendix B has the steps. This clears out a corrupted queue and it works surprisingly often.
steps.label: Remove the printer and add…

steps.text: If it is a small printer on your own desk: check both ends of the cable and the power. Then swap the cable — come and get one from us, we keep a box of them and we would rather give you a cable than book an appointment.
steps.label: It is a small printer on your?

flows.name: Appendix A — “It will not print”: the Tier 1 troubleshooting ladder

flows.head: Appendix B — Adding a printer, step by step

steps.text: Find the printer’s name. It is on a sticker on the machine. If there is no sticker, tell the service desk — that is our fault and we will fix it.
steps.label: Find the printer’s name

steps.text: Click the Start button and open Settings.
steps.label: Click the Start button and open…

steps.text: Choose Bluetooth & devices, then Printers & scanners.
steps.label: Choose Bluetooth & devices, then Printers…

steps.text: Click Add device, and wait about thirty seconds. Nearby printers appear in the list.
steps.label: Click Add device, and wait about…

steps.text: When you see the one you want, click Add device next to it. Windows will fetch what it needs, which takes a minute or two.
steps.label: You see the one you want?

gate.cond: you see the one you want
gate.then: click Add device next to it

steps.text: If your printer does not appear in the list, click “The printer that I want isn’t listed” and stop there — the rest of that screen needs information you should not have to know. Send us the printer’s name and we will add it for you, usually the same day.
steps.label: Your printer does not appear?

gate.cond: your printer does not appear in the list
gate.then: click “The printer that I want isn’t listed” and stop there — the rest of that screen needs information you should not have to know

steps.text: Print a test page. In the same Printers & scanners screen, click your new printer, then Printer properties, then Print Test Page. Do this now rather than at the moment you need it.
steps.label: Print a test page

steps.text: Open System Settings from the Apple menu.
steps.label: Open System Settings from the Apple…

steps.text: Choose Printers & Scanners.
steps.label: Choose Printers & Scanners

steps.text: Click Add Printer, Scanner or Fax.
steps.label: Click Add Printer, Scanner or Fax

steps.text: Wait for the list to populate, choose your printer, and click Add.
steps.label: Wait for the list to populate…

steps.text: Print a test page from any document.
steps.label: Print a test page from any…

title: Conference & Meeting Room AV Standard
subtitle: Room technology fails in front of an audience. The cost is not the repair — it is forty people watching. Written for the ninety seconds that actually matter, and for the person standing at the lectern.
tierText: Tier 2 — meeting room and AV emergencies are Tier 2 work. Where a separate AV or room support desk exists, this document attaches to it rather than replacing it. Tier 1 takes the call and runs the ladder in §6. Tier 3 owns the Teams Rooms tenant configuration. Tier 4 owns room investment and the §11 replacement decisions.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
approver: [ unassigned — recommend the IT lead, with whoever owns scheduling on §4.3 and §10 ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and after each start-of-season readiness sweep (§10).

callouts.title: The guaranteed way not to fail in front of an audience is to have walked in twenty minutes earlier.
lines: Twenty minutes, not five. Five minutes is enough to discover a problem and not enough to solve it, which is worse than not knowing — you now start the session rattled and behind.
Nothing else in this document comes close to the value of this one habit. Every step below takes seconds; the whole check is under ten minutes in a room that is working.

steps.text: Turn the display on and select the input. Confirm you can see your own desktop on the big screen. This is step one because it is the most common failure and because everything after it depends on it.
steps.label: Turn the display on and select…

steps.text: Connect with your own cable and your own laptop — the ones you will use. A room that works with the resident PC tells you nothing about whether it works with your machine.
steps.label: Connect with your own cable…

steps.text: Open the actual file from where it actually lives. Not a copy, not a similar deck. If it is going to fail to open, or fail to find its embedded video, you want that at 8:40.
steps.label: Open the actual file from where…

steps.text: Play something with sound and listen to it in the room. Audio is the check nobody does and the failure everybody remembers. Confirm you can hear it from the back, not just from the lectern.
steps.label: Play something with sound and listen…

steps.text: If the session is hybrid or recorded, join the meeting from the room and confirm the room camera and the room microphone are the selected devices — not the laptop’s. This is the single most common hybrid failure: the far end sees a ceiling and hears a lectern.
steps.label: The session is hybrid or recorded?

gate.cond: the session is hybrid or recorded
gate.then: join the meeting from the room and confirm the room camera and the room microphone are the selected devices — not the laptop’s

steps.text: Ring a colleague into the meeting for thirty seconds and ask them whether they can see and hear the room. Thirty seconds. It is the only test that tests the whole chain.
steps.label: Ring a colleague into the meeting…

steps.text: Have the material in two places: in OneDrive or the Team, and a copy on the local drive or a USB stick. The network is not a thing you get to blame at 9:02, and a local copy costs you nothing.
steps.label: Have the material in two places

steps.text: Find the card (Appendix A), note the room number and the number to call, and know where the light switches and the blinds are. Small things, and they are the ones that go wrong in a strange room.
steps.label: Find the card (Appendix A), note…

steps.text: For anything genuinely high-stakes, book Tier 2 attendance when you book the room, not on the day. A booked attendance is a planned half-hour; an emergency is a technician abandoning something else and arriving after it mattered (§7).
steps.label: For anything genuinely high-stakes, book Tier…

callouts.title: The three-minute rule
lines: If it is not fixed in three minutes, stop and fall back. Three minutes of a presenter crouched behind a lectern with their back to the room does more damage than the fault did, and the fourth minute never works either.

Call it in, run the session, and let somebody fix the room afterwards when there is nobody in it. That is a better outcome for the audience and a much better outcome for the room, because a fault diagnosed calmly gets fixed properly instead of patched under pressure.
Nobody has ever been criticised for running a session without slides. Everybody remembers the fifteen minutes.

steps.text: The display input. Press the source or input button until you see your screen. Around half of all room faults are this, and it takes ten seconds. Do it before anything else, every single time.
steps.label: The display input

steps.text: The cable. Unplug both ends and plug them back in firmly. Then, if there is a spare in the room, use the spare. Twenty seconds.
steps.label: The cable

steps.text: Wake the room. Touch the console, move the resident PC’s mouse, press a key. A room that looks dead is usually asleep.
steps.label: Wake the room

steps.text: Audio: check three places, in this order — the volume in the application, the volume in the operating system, and the room’s own volume control. It is almost always one of the first two, and it is almost always muted rather than low.
steps.label: Audio

steps.text: In a meeting, check the device selection. Open the audio and video settings inside Teams or Zoom and confirm the room camera and room microphone are chosen. If the meeting was started on the laptop rather than in the room, this will be wrong by default.
steps.label: In a meeting, check the device…

steps.text: Restart the console or the room system — but look at the clock first. It takes three to five minutes and it is worth it only if you have them. If you do not, go to step 7 now.
steps.label: Restart the console or the room…

steps.text: Fall back deliberately, and say so out loud. Present from the laptop screen, turn it toward the room, use the whiteboard, or carry on with the material and share the deck afterwards. Then call. This is a supported action and not a failure — it is the right decision, and it is in this document so that nobody feels they are improvising when they take it.
steps.label: Fall back deliberately, and say…

flows.head: 9. Room and endpoint telephony — the ninety-day ticket

callouts.title: The ninety-day ticket, because it is the clearest example of what an absent document costs
lines: “Request for Help: Re-registering Teams Desk Phone”. SLA target passed. Still open, still in violation, three months later, and re-notifying hourly along with the rest of the P3 backlog.

Ninety days. Re-registering a Teams desk phone is a twenty-minute job for somebody who has done it once. It did not age because it was hard, or because it was deprioritised in favour of something more important. It aged because it fell between the telephony service and the device in the room: no document said whose job it was, and no runbook said how, so it belonged to nobody and there was nothing to hand to whoever picked it up.

That is what a missing P3 procedure costs — not a slow response, but no response at all, for three months, on something trivial. GOV-06 §9.3 names this kind of ticket as the test case for re-baselining the backlog: it is either accepted with a real date, redirected, or closed as will-not-do with the requester told. It is not left as it is.

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Establish what the device is signed in as. This is the diagnosis, and it is almost always the answer: a device signed in with a departing person’s account, with a shared credential, or with a personal account instead of the resource account it should hold.
steps.label: Establish what the device is signed…

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Confirm the correct identity for the device. A common-area or room phone signs in as a resource account under ACC-08, licensed for it (M365-20). A personal desk phone signs in as its user. A device inheriting a leaver’s account is an ACC-01 §7.2 gap and should be recorded as one.
steps.label: Confirm the correct identity…

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Sign the device out cleanly at the device where it is responsive, or remotely from the Teams admin centre where it is not.
steps.label: Sign the device out cleanly…

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Sign in by device code from the admin centre rather than by typing a password into a handset. It is faster, it does not expose the credential in a room, and it works with the modern authentication requirements the handset may not fully support.
steps.label: Sign in by device code…

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Update firmware while you are there. A handset several versions behind is the cause of a class of registration faults that look like account faults, and it will otherwise be the next ticket.
steps.label: Update firmware while you are there

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Test: an inbound call, an outbound call, and voicemail. Three tests, two minutes, and they are what distinguish a closed ticket from a returning one.
steps.label: Test

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Record the device, its account, its firmware and its location in the asset register. A telephony device that is not in the register is a device that will produce another ninety-day ticket, because nobody will know what it is meant to be.
steps.label: Record the device, its account…

steps.sub: 9.1 Desk and room phone re-registration — the runbook that was missing
steps.text: Where the device cannot be recovered, say so and replace it. Three attempts across three weeks is worse for everyone than a replacement handset in week one.
steps.label: The device cannot be recovered?

gate.cond: the device cannot be recovered
gate.then: say so and replace it

flows.name: Room and endpoint telephony — the ninety-day ticket

callouts.title: Being honest about the capacity this needs
lines: A genuine check of a single room takes fifteen to twenty-five minutes. A hundred rooms is three to four person-days, in the fortnight that is already the busiest of the year for onboarding preparation (GOV-06).

So the plan is a prioritised partial sweep with a published list, not an unpublished intention to do all of them. A partial sweep everybody knows about is more useful than a complete sweep that was planned and did not happen — and it is the version that can be repeated next year.

If the organization wants every room swept, that is a resourcing decision for Tier 4, and it is a small one: it is a week of a Front Door technician’s time with a checklist and somebody to escalate to.

steps.text: Two weeks before the start of a busy season, Tier 2 begins the sweep. Appendix B is the checklist, one per room, and it is completed in the room rather than from memory.
steps.label: Two weeks before the start…

steps.text: Sequence by risk, not by room number. Rooms booked in the first week first, then R3 and R4 rooms, then everything else. This is the step that makes a partial sweep useful.
steps.label: Sequence by risk, not by room…

steps.text: Every check is a real check. Play audio, plug in a laptop, join a test meeting in an R3 room. A visual inspection confirms the equipment is present and confirms nothing about whether it works.
steps.label: Every check is a real check

steps.text: Faults found go into the register (§11) with the room number, and anything that cannot be fixed before the busy season goes to Tier 4 as a list with costs attached — not as an assurance that it is being looked at.
steps.label: Faults found go into the register…

steps.text: Publish which rooms were swept and when. This is the honest part: the department cannot sweep every room every quarter, so it publishes what it did. Someone presenting in an unswept room can then do the §5 check themselves, which they cannot do if they believe the room was checked.
steps.label: Publish which rooms were swept…

steps.text: Repeat, abbreviated, at the start of each busy season and before any period when the organization hosts external visitors.
steps.label: Repeat, abbreviated, at the start…

appendices.head: Appendix A — The presenter quick card
rows: 1. Press the INPUT or SOURCE button
Keep pressing until you see your own screen. This is the answer about half the time. Ten seconds.
2. Reseat the cable
Unplug both ends, push them back in firmly. If there is a spare cable in the room, try it.
3. Wake everything up
Touch the console. Move the mouse. Press a key. Rooms sleep.
4. Check your laptop is sending
Windows key + P, then choose Duplicate. On a Mac, look in Displays.

title: Knowledge Base Article Standard & End-User Guide Format
subtitle: An SOP is for the person who does the work. An article is for the person with the problem. This is how the second one gets written, published, and kept true — starting from whatever guide library you already have.
tierText: Tier 2 — Advanced Technical Services writes and maintains most articles, because Tier 2 is where the escalated version of every Tier 1 question already lands. Tier 1 identifies what is missing and is the primary consumer. Tier 3 writes for tiers 3 and 4. Tier 4 approves publication of anything stating an organization position rather than a procedure.

review: Annually. The article review cycle in §8 is quarterly and is a different thing — do not conflate them.

flows.head: 9. How a ticket becomes an article

callouts.title: The third identical ticket is a documentation defect, not a support event
lines: Two people asking the same question is a coincidence. Three is a pattern, and continuing to answer it individually is a decision to keep paying for it — forty times a quarter, at fifteen minutes each, for as long as the organization operates the service.
So the third occurrence stops being a support event and becomes a defect with an owner and a due date, exactly like a bug. That reframing is the entire mechanism of this section.

steps.text: Tier 1 or Tier 2 flags the third occurrence, against the ticket category (GOV-02). The flag is a field, not a conversation, and it takes ten seconds.
steps.label: Tier 1 or Tier 2 flags…

steps.text: The flag creates one article task with a NAMED OWNER and a DUE DATE. Not a backlog entry, not a note in a meeting. An unowned documentation task is a documentation task that will not happen, and the FAQ ticket in §1 is the evidence.
steps.label: The flag creates one article task…

steps.text: The default owner is the tier that resolves the ticket, because they already know the answer and writing it down is fifteen minutes rather than an hour of research.
steps.label: The default owner is the tier…

steps.text: Answer the third ticket normally. The article does not hold up the person who asked; it prevents the fourth person needing to.
steps.label: Answer the third ticket normally

steps.text: Publish within ten coverage days of the flag (§14). Then reply to the requester with the link — which is both a courtesy and a test of whether the article is any good.
steps.label: Publish within ten coverage days…

steps.text: Monthly, check the top ticket categories by volume against the article list. A category in the top ten with no published article is a gap with a name written against it, reported with the GOV-02 numbers.
steps.label: Monthly, check the top ticket categories…

steps.sub: 9.3 The FAQ case — what to do with a ticket like the one in §1
steps.text: Break the ticket into its constituent questions. One article each.
steps.label: Break the ticket into its constituent…

steps.sub: 9.3 The FAQ case — what to do with a ticket like the one in §1
steps.text: Write the two or three that are most asked. Do not attempt all six before publishing any — a partial answer published this week beats a complete one that never ships.
steps.label: Write the two or three…

steps.sub: 9.3 The FAQ case — what to do with a ticket like the one in §1
steps.text: Reply to the staff who raised it with the links, an honest acknowledgement of how long it has taken, and a note of which questions are still coming.
steps.label: Reply to the staff who raised…

steps.sub: 9.3 The FAQ case — what to do with a ticket like the one in §1
steps.text: Close it. A six-week-old ticket converted into three permanent articles is a good trade, and it is the trade the department needs to start making routinely rather than exceptionally.
steps.label: Close it

callouts.title: One honest caveat before this is published as a control
lines: The Microsoft 365 group naming policy and the group expiration policy are both licensed features, counted against the members of the groups they apply to. Tier 3 confirms the organization’s entitlement covers the population before §4 and §8 are described to anyone as enforced.

If the entitlement is not there, §4 and §8 are enforced by procedure and by the monthly report instead — which is materially weaker, and the document should say so rather than imply a control that is not switched on.
ACTION: Tier 3 to confirm and report to Tier 4 within 30 days of approval. Recorded against M365-21.

title: Teams Meetings, Recording & Guest Participation
subtitle: One stated rule for recording and consent, where recordings and transcripts actually end up, and who is allowed into your meeting.
tierText: Tier 1 — the front door answers almost everything in this document, and §9 is written to be worked through at Tier 1 without escalating. Tier 3 owns the meeting-policy configuration; Tier 4 owns §2 and §7.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]

version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman

callouts.title: Open — owner: senior leadership, with HR and the Head of IT
lines: The organization has no published policy on session recording that IT is aware of. Absent one, individual presenters are deciding it session by session, which is inconsistent for participants and offers no protection to presenters either.
ACTION: senior leadership to state the policy position. IT holds the technical rules above in the meantime and will align this section to whatever is decided.

steps.text: A session recording lives in the team’s Team or site, never in the presenter’s OneDrive. A presenter changing role or leaving takes a personal OneDrive with them (§3, M365-16 §5), and months of recordings goes with it.
steps.label: A session recording lives…

steps.text: A session recording is not shared, linked or posted anywhere reachable by people outside the intended audience. The people in the recording did not consent to a wider audience by attending a session.
steps.label: A session recording is not shared…

steps.text: The presenter tells the room before recording begins, at the first session and again whenever it resumes, and offers a way to take part without appearing on camera. This is §2 applied to a room where the participants cannot easily object.
steps.label: The presenter tells the room before…

steps.text: Requests to release a session recording to anybody outside the intended audience — a relative, an outside employer, an investigator, another department — go to the department that owns those records. Where a formal process is involved they go through M365-16 §8. IT does not release a session recording on request, however reasonable the request sounds.
steps.label: Requests to release a session recording…

steps.text: Where a recording is required as an accommodation, that is arranged through the office responsible for accessibility, and the technical delivery is what IT provides.
steps.label: A recording is required as an accommodation?

title: Teams Phone, Desk Phone & Voicemail Standard
subtitle: Who gets a number, how a desk phone is re-registered, and where an emergency call says you are. Written because a request with no procedure has no owner.
tierText: Tier 2 — Advanced Technical Services owns phones, devices and the §4 runbook. Tier 1 triages from Appendix A. Tier 3 owns numbering, routing and the emergency location map; Tier 4 owns the entitlement decision at §2 and the compliance position at §8.
owner: [ unassigned — name an owner in your shop ]
version: 1.0 · Known Good edition, by Kevin Zelman
review: Annually, and after any change to the site network that moves subnets, switches or access points (§8).

callouts.title: IT does not sign in as the user. Ever.
lines: The device-code flow exists precisely so that the user completes their own authentication. A technician who asks for a password to get a phone working has done the thing the organization tells every member of staff nobody from IT will ever do (ACC-15 §4), and has undone a control that took years to establish.
If the user is not available, the phone waits. It is a telephone.

steps.text: Establish what is actually being reported. “The phone does not work” covers at least four distinct faults: it shows a sign-in screen, it shows the wrong person’s name, it is signed in but takes no calls, or it is dead. Ask, and write the answer in the ticket.
steps.label: Establish what is actually being reported

steps.text: CHECK THE ACCOUNT BEFORE TOUCHING THE PHONE. Is the user licensed for Teams Phone, do they have a number assigned, and is enterprise voice enabled? A phone that will not register because a licence was reclaimed looks exactly like a hardware fault and is diagnosed as one for an hour (M365-20).
steps.label: CHECK THE ACCOUNT BEFORE TOUCHING…

steps.text: Check the network. The phone has an IP address, reaches DNS and the internet, and — where it is powered over Ethernet — the switch port is delivering power. A phone on a port that was re-patched during other work is a common and entirely undramatic cause.
steps.label: Check the network

steps.text: RECORD THE FIRMWARE VERSION NOW, before changing anything. Old firmware is the second most common cause of a phone that will not register, and it is the one nobody writes down, so nobody knows whether the estate is current.
steps.label: RECORD THE FIRMWARE VERSION NOW, before…

steps.text: Sign out cleanly on the device before signing in again. Signing in over a stale session is how a phone ends up half-registered, showing the previous user’s name and taking nobody’s calls.
steps.label: Sign out cleanly on the device…

steps.text: Generate the device code and have the USER complete the web sign-in with their own credentials and their own MFA (§4.2). Stay with them; the flow times out and the code expires.
steps.label: Generate the device code and have…

steps.text: IF THE CODE IS REJECTED OR THE SIGN-IN LOOPS, stop retrying. Two things cause this and neither is the phone: a Conditional Access policy blocking the device-code authentication flow, or the account being in scope of an MFA requirement the handset cannot satisfy. Both are Tier 3. A rushed phishing-resistant MFA rollout is a classic way to leave users stuck in an MFA setup loop, so this failure mode is common.
steps.label: THE CODE IS REJECTED?

gate.cond: THE CODE IS REJECTED OR THE SIGN-IN LOOPS
gate.then: stop retrying

steps.text: Once signed in, update the firmware, then restart, then re-test. Updating after a successful sign-in rather than before means a failed update does not leave an unregistered phone.
steps.label: Update the firmware, then restart…

steps.text: Test properly, in this order: internal call in, internal call out, EXTERNAL call in on the DID, external call out, hold, transfer, and voicemail. A phone tested only by dialling a colleague is a phone half-tested.
steps.label: Test properly, in this order

steps.text: CONFIRM THE EMERGENCY ADDRESS on the device and in the register (§8). A phone that has moved desk, floor or building has moved emergency address, and this is the step that gets skipped because the phone is now working and everyone is relieved.
steps.label: CONFIRM THE EMERGENCY ADDRESS…

steps.text: Update the DID register and the device record: firmware version, sign-in date, location, emergency address.
steps.label: Update the DID register…

steps.text: Close the ticket with the CAUSE recorded, not “resolved”. The cause column of §4.4 is built from those entries, and without them the next occurrence starts from nothing again — which is how the desk-phone ticket happened (GOV-02).
steps.label: Close the ticket with the CAUSE…

flows.head: 8. Emergency calling and dynamic emergency address

callouts.title: A softphone that reports the wrong location is worse than no phone at all.
lines: If a member of staff dials 911 from Teams on a laptop and the call carries a static address registered against their number, responders are sent to that address. If the person has taken the laptop to another building, to a different site, or home, the address is wrong — and it is wrong with the full confidence of a system. Somebody who dialled 911 from their mobile would at least have been asked where they were.
This is a site safety matter, not a telephony configuration matter, and it is the section of this document that should be read by somebody outside IT.

NAMED OWNER: the network owner in IT owns the network location map (§8.2). Security owns the notification recipients and the response (§8.3). The Head of IT owns the compliance position (§8.1). Unowned, this section does not operate.

steps.sub: 8.3 What has to be built and maintained
steps.text: A network location map: every site subnet, wireless access point and switch port mapped to a civic address with a building and, where possible, a floor. This is real work, it belongs to whoever owns the network, and it is the piece that is usually never done because it is nobody’s single job.
steps.label: A network location map

steps.sub: 8.3 What has to be built and maintained
steps.text: An emergency address on every number in the register, set at assignment and confirmed at every §4 re-registration (§4.3 step 10).
steps.label: An emergency address on every number…

steps.sub: 8.3 What has to be built and maintained
steps.text: Emergency call notification to Security, so that when 911 is dialled from an organization device the security desk is told immediately and can meet responders at the right door. Security names the recipients and confirms they are monitored.
steps.label: Emergency call notification to Security, so…

steps.sub: 8.3 What has to be built and maintained
steps.text: A test, annually, with Security and with the carrier, using the carrier’s test procedure and never by dialling 911 speculatively. Record the result; an untested emergency configuration is an assumption.
steps.label: A test, annually, with Security and…

steps.sub: 8.3 What has to be built and maintained
steps.text: A re-test whenever the network changes in a way that moves subnets, access points or switches. This is why §8 is in the review trigger in the control block.
steps.label: A re-test whenever the network changes…

flows.name: Emergency calling and dynamic emergency address

appendices.head: Appendix A — Tier 1 / Tier 2 triage table
rows: “My desk phone is asking me to sign in”
Confirm the licence and number are in place, then run the §4.3 device-code sign-in with the user present. Most are closed here.
Tier 2 if the code is rejected
Firmware version, the exact on-screen message, whether the password was recently reset
“My phone has no power / no display”
Check the patch lead and the wall port; try a known-good port. Do not swap the phone first.
Tier 2
Port and room number, whether other devices on that port work
“People cannot reach me on my number”
Confirm a number is assigned and enterprise voice is on. Test an inbound external call yourself rather than believing the report.
Tier 2
The number dialled, what the caller heard, time of the test
“The caller could not hear me / audio kept breaking up”
Record time, both parties, direction and whether it was internal or external. Do not swap hardware.
Tier 3
Times, parties, direction, device type, network location
“Nobody answers the department number”
Call it yourself and follow it through the menu. Find where it lands.
Tier 2, and tell the queue owner
Where the call actually ended up, and the queue’s named owner

Check §2. Where it is not an entitlement, explain the alternative — Teams calling, or the department queue — rather than opening a request that will be declined later.

Role, reason, whether it will be published, building and room

Confirm it is arriving in the mailbox as mail (§7). Check the mailbox before the phone.
Tier 2
Whether any voicemail arrives, and whether the greeting plays to a caller

Update the location and the emergency address in the register. This is not optional and it is not deferred (§8).
